translations.text: God’s anger was stirred up: namely, all these schisms, quarrels, and divisions, and along with these, frequent and bitter persecutions.
And we see imprisonments and harsh bonds. All these, too, are among the birth pangs of the end.
For our Savior himself was already proclaiming at that time, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near to you.”
Again, he gave clear signs, saying plainly, “When you see all these things happening, know that it has reached the door.”
Again, he also taught his disciples beforehand and informed them about the things now happening among us—not only that great company of apostles,
but also all the disciples who came after them, down to our own day—saying this: “Beware of people.
"For they will hand you over to the courts, and in their synagogues they will scourge you."
And they will bring you before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations.
But when they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you will say, for what you are to say will be given to you at that hour.
For it is not you who speak, but your Father’s Spirit speaking through you. Brother will hand brother over to death, and a father his child.
Children will rise up against their parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by everyone because of my name.”
These are the things that we clearly see coming upon all the members of the church and being fulfilled even now, in this time,
as we endure these conflicts and evils, not from outsiders and pagans, but from those who are themselves also considered Christians,
and who freely commit pagan deeds against their fellow Christians, without the restraints of the fear of God and without mercy, cruelly and savagely, without restraint.
Because of all these things, then: after the first written history, in two parts, which we finished earlier with much labour over a long time,
the histories of the church, as far as we were able, in twelve books, all distinguished by different headings,
beginning with the times of Julius Caesar and the other early Roman rulers,
we then gathered and arranged the church histories in sequence, down to the sixth year of the reign of this later Justin, the son of Justinian’s sister.
We also dealt with King Justin’s own zeal and concern for the unity of the church, from the beginning of his reign down to his sixth year,
we also bear witness to this carefully and diligently, holding to the truth in the events we have already made known.
But now, again, because we have seen a violent storm suddenly rise with force and fury, thundering with the might of its frequent and numerous waves because of our sins,
against the sound ship of the whole church of the orthodox, we too have therefore been moved to set down a record,
even if we present only a few of these things, although the times themselves hem us in on every side and hinder us in many ways,
and do all they can to prevent us from undertaking even a brief narration of the events of church history that are now happening once again.
We are setting down in a record a few of these many things, and we will also include them in this third account, for the information of those who come after us.
Even though I was well aware that the times of the world had already run their course and were passing away [?],
so that these things may be known clearly and reliably also to all the others who come afterward, even within the short time
and that this turmoil [?] was what remained for this world, we have set things down in brief records as knowledge for those who come after us.
Now, to begin the narratives of this book, the mournful words of the lamentations of the sorrowful prophet Jeremiah would have been fitting,
with which he once lamented and wept over Jerusalem and over its people who fell by the sword.
In the same way, let us now lament and weep over the things that have happened at this time in the church of God because of our many wrongdoings and sins.
Likewise Isaiah, renowned among the prophets, would himself cry out at the top of his voice without holding back,
and raise his voice like a trumpet, seeing this harsh punishment that has overtaken the church of God.
He would also add and repeat, saying, “Every head is in pain, and every heart is in sorrow.
From the sole of the foot to the top of the head, there is no sound place in it, but only wounds, bruises, and swollen sores.
"Not to be bound up, nor bandaged, nor softened with oil."
And again, he who tells of the suffering says: "The earth mourned and sat in mourning; it mourned and sat, and the world was made to mourn."
The heights of the earth lament, and the earth has become like its inhabitants.” It would therefore have been fitting for such holy men to grieve mournfully with us
over this great wrath that, because of our sins, was suddenly sent against the church of God, just as it once was against Jerusalem.
about the calamities of the forces [?] that roared from on high, shook, and distressed the whole people of the believers,
who had been living peacefully and quietly and enjoying themselves for a long time in the imperial city and throughout its surrounding districts,
until the sixth year of the reign of the victorious Justin, when suddenly an onslaught of wrath struck all the congregations of the orthodox church,
and it swept them away and scattered them to every wind. I have too little time to write about these things and bring them to completion.
For during a long period of more than forty years, all the congregations of the entire orthodox church
They had been living in quiet and peace in this great imperial city and in all the surrounding area:
Quite openly, freely, without restriction and without fear, all the congregations of believers were gathering everywhere
and celebrating all the sacraments and church services. Suddenly, during the holy days of the forty-day fast,
on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, through the zeal and fierce malice of the man who held authority over the church of the imperial city,
Now this John was from Sirimis, a village of Syria, and he made many accusations against the whole party of the orthodox:
the victorious Justin was stirred to fierce anger, and with threats of great fury he ordered all the meeting places of all the believers to be shut.
And all the altars in all of them were to be torn down, and all the priests and their chief priests were to be arrested,
and thrown into prison. All those who used to assemble in them were to be driven away and harassed, so that they would no longer assemble.
And other things of this kind were commanded and decreed in great anger. Yet although, from long before until that time, peacefully and quietly throughout the whole of it—
Chapter Nine. Together with those who sent me to you, why do you sit as a Christian, yet judge the servants of God like a pagan?
You are not among living human beings unless you quickly burn me, a feeble old man, and eat me roasted.
When the prefect heard these things, he was moved by respect for his old age, and gave orders, and they took him out of his presence
They brought him to the bishop. The bishop, on his own authority [?], had him sent to prison in Heraclea, a city of Thrace.
He remained there for two years, without being allowed to see any of his acquaintances.
Since he was not given a change of clothing, he was swarming with countless lice.
One of his disciples went out and brought him a change of clothing, but permission was refused for it to be given to him even through someone else. Afterward he became deathly ill.
And he forbade, under anathema, his being buried by adherents of the council, or any one of them conducting a service or offering prayer over him.
And so the orthodox commanders of the Roman army who happened to be there brought him out and buried him with many candles and spices.
They wrapped his body and bore it in procession as that of a great martyr. They also voiced reproaches and denunciations against the persecution of people like these.
Some of the believers in the city planned to go out and take the holy man's body.
Also the monasteries of men and of women that are in the imperial city and in all its surrounding area and districts:
some of which had large numbers of inhabitants, especially the women's monasteries whose inhabitants had been persecuted from the beginning,
from Antioch, Isauria, Cilicia and Cappadocia, and the other regions, which had been gathered by the late Empress Theodora, whose soul is at rest:
Some of those monasteries had more than three hundred brothers. But the storm and whirlwind of persecution suddenly overtook these too.
and a smoky cloud and bewildering darkness of persecution covered them. That is, clerics, together with laymen and prison officials,
and officers accompanied by the staff of the city's prefect, were sent against them and surrounded the monasteries with savage fury.
Like a pack of wolves entering and falling upon a fold of lambs, they too rushed destructively into each of these monasteries,
upon Christ's ewes, while the clerics carried their Eucharistic offerings and dragged and pulled the women, so that they would come and receive communion from them.
But all the women fled like birds before hawks and hid in the inner rooms,
wailing and saying, “We cannot receive communion from the Council of Chalcedon,
which divides Christ our God into two natures after the union, and teaches a quaternity instead of the Holy Trinity.”
And so, with blows and pulling, they dragged them forward to receive communion, with their hands held above their heads.
While they wailed, they were carried by their arms, crying out with lamentation, stamping, shouting loudly, and trying to flee.
And so the communion offering was forcibly put into their mouths, while they said many things amid cries of lamentation.
Some of the women threw themselves face down on the ground and cursed anyone who demanded that they take communion by force.
And so they subdued some of them. All those who stood against them and would not be persuaded, they separated out, dragged off, and drove out of their monasteries.
Each was handed over into the hands of the Roman guards (taxeotai), while the guards pulled them about and abused them.
They were taken into the city and distributed among houses and various prisons. And, according to what was being reported,
many men committed acts of sexual violence against them like frenzied stallions—things that, for our part, should be covered in silence,
since their case is reserved for the righteous Judge, who will judge their case and exact vengeance for them.
And so these things were done in this savage and barbarous manner in all the monasteries, both those of men and those of women.
Now John was the instigator, promoter, and perpetrator of all these evils.
He was the one already mentioned as the head of the city's church. Out of the abundant bitterness of his wickedness,
he would go in and bring accusations, inflaming the emperor's anger against the entire community of the faithful. Then he would come out, having obtained authorization to act against them.
Through those who supported his wishes, he poured out all the filth of his wickedness upon every order of the faithful everywhere.
Nor did he act only within his own city and jurisdiction: he also wrote to other regions, causing disturbances and stirring up turmoil, persecutions, and evil deeds.
Thus he now went out in person and made the rounds of all the monasteries of men and women, and also of private houses,
compelling and pressuring people to enter into communion with him. As for those who opposed him, whether men or women, whether monks
or clergy or nuns, he would issue orders in fierce and merciless anger,
sending them all away, one by one, to be confined in monasteries, and imposing harsh sentences of death upon them.
He even managed to mislead and stir up the victorious sovereigns themselves, inducing them to be drawn in by him and to go out one after another to make the rounds of the monasteries.
First he himself would go with his clergy and hold assemblies and celebrations of the Eucharist in the monasteries, proclaiming in them the divisive council.
He installed his own portraits in them and appointed clergy there to offer the Eucharist every Sunday and on every feast and commemoration.
Then, on another day after him, the emperor himself would make the rounds of those monasteries. After him, on yet another day, the empress would do the same.
They also gave gifts and assigned daily allowances to those who had yielded or were yielding to them.
But those who resisted they sent into exile and into harsh prisons.
or they were handed over without mercy to the torturers in the praetoria.
and were furiously subjected to scourging and bitter, harsh afflictions, with bitter rage.
Now that bishop was filled with a spirit of hostile zeal and was driven by vehemence and anger.
Just as that man was blind in his physical eyesight, so this man was blinded in his soul by the passion of hostility and grew bold like a drunken man.
After he had managed, through every kind of savage tyranny and compulsion, to subdue many priests of the Orthodox and forcibly bring them into communion with him,
and after they had come forward and been received by him in their priestly rank, the presbyters being received by him as presbyters,
they received communion alongside his own presbyters in full accordance with their rank and sat in order with them in the sanctuary; and the deacons likewise,
they too performing all the duties of the diaconate together with his own deacons—not merely once or twice,
but as many as thirty-six times, at all the liturgical assemblies of the feast and those afterward, serving with him in their own priestly rank,
and fulfilling all the duties of the priesthood—then afterward a savage idea arose in his mind, as though he were a mere young boy.
Frenziedly carried away by pride and drunk with authority and self-exaltation, he issued this command:
“We command that all those from among our opponents who have submitted to us be stripped of their former priesthood and become priests anew through us.”

And so he then stripped them all of their priesthood, after they had served as priests with him and before him thirty-six times in their former priesthood, the one they had received from the Orthodox.
He himself ordained anew all those who had entered into communion with him, while they were disturbed and agitated, anathematizing him and reviling him and his unlawful priesthood.
He appointed some of them to the clergy of the church itself, while many, even among his own supporters, were finding fault
with this transgression of the law, contrary to all canonical order, which he had wickedly and savagely committed.
Nor was the evil that he had personally done and carried through enough for him: he also wrote to the various regions and urged the bishops
to act in the same way as he had. He was devising schemes and contriving ways not to be the only one blamed and accused
for the unlawful and disorderly things he had done, but to have others implicated with him under the same blame and accusation.
Now it had been revealed beforehand to a certain blessed and virtuous man in a vision of the night what would soon, without delay, actually happen in the church of God.
For he saw a great mountain extending over a vast distance.
On its southern side there was a great planting of many churches, built in a row, one after another, extending a great distance.
They were closely set, beautiful, splendid, and numerous. He saw that suddenly John, the bishop of the imperial city, arrived
with clergy and a large crowd accompanying him. He rushed violently upon them and began tearing down and demolishing all these churches.
He also tore down and demolished the altars of them all, until he had finished with them. And indeed, immediately after this vision, a few days later,
This very thing was fulfilled in practice when he went out and uprooted and overthrew all the numerous congregations of the churches of the faithful,
in that city and throughout its surrounding districts, in accordance with the revelation and the vision that had previously been revealed. It soon came openly into effect.
Now this Paul, whom we also mentioned briefly above, was from the region of Caria.
who had been made and named bishop of Aphrodisias, the metropolis of Caria: a good and simple old man. He was living quietly in his monastery:
as we explained earlier, John the patriarch sent for him, arrested him, put him in irons, and imprisoned him in his own episcopal residence.
By putting him under severe pressure, he forced him into communion with himself. Then he sent him out to the province.
He wrote and instructed the man who was in that city to depose him from his bishopric and ordain him anew as bishop in Antioch, a city of Caria.
This was in fact carried out in deed. They released him, and once they believed they had stripped him of his priesthood, they made him a layman, as it were, all over again.
Thus he became an object of disgrace and ridicule both to those people and to his own people. His clergy used to call him ‘twice-dyed.’
Then he also sent for this old man, Elisha the bishop, and brought him from the monastery called Beth Dios, where he had been confined.
He imprisoned him too in his own episcopal residence. As they subjected him to great pressure to force him into communion with him, he tried to devise a way,
that even so he might escape from his hands. But he wanted to send him to Sardis, the metropolis of Lydia.
When he wanted to depose him from his bishopric and ordain him too anew, Elisha opposed him, saying,
‘Although I am unworthy, I have been ordained bishop by the orthodox. You shall certainly not ordain me anew.
But if you think it is in accordance with church order to depose me and ordain me anew,
then first undo the baptism with which I was baptized, and then perform both.’ John said to him deceitfully,
‘I am only putting a cloak on you.’ But when Elisha would not be persuaded at all or submit to him, and would not accept his words,
he became angry with him and sent him to be imprisoned in another monastery, called Beth Abraham. A harsh sentence was pronounced against him.
He remained there in distress for a long time. Eventually he fell seriously ill and asked to go to the hot baths. He was allowed to leave under guard.
Now while the powerful John was arrogantly exalting himself, trampling on and violating all the church’s regulations,
he sent to the island called Platea, to which he had banished Stephen the bishop.
Stephen was one of those who had firmly rebuked him shortly before over the annulment of ordination. Against this man he sent clergy and imperial guards.
He ordered them to make him a ball [?] (to be tossed about) until he vomited blood, unless he was persuaded to join their communion.
So he was tossed about like a ball [?] among twelve excubitors (imperial guards), until he collapsed among them and fell silent.
By then he was as good as dead. When they saw that he had collapsed, lay motionless, and was close to death, they ran and brought four jars of water and splashed it over him.
After a long time, however, he regained consciousness and came back to life as though from the dead. And so, under compulsion, he was forced into communion with them.

This was especially because some of the faithful who had been sending him what he needed were discovered, arrested, and imprisoned on his account, and preparations were being made to attack and plunder them.
And so they took him and went into the city, and there was a great deal of upheaval among them. And under compulsion he entered into communion with them.
Afterward, John himself was insisting that he be deposed and ordained again as bishop of the island of Cyprus.
But he disputed with him and argued against him, stirred up a disturbance, and began crying out in distress:
“If you wish to strip me of the priesthood of the Orthodox and ordain me again, first release me from baptism as well,
and baptize me again first. Then you may strip me of the priesthood and make me a priest again.
For as the Lord God lives, unless you baptize me again, I will never, ever agree.”
And so, when a great disturbance arose among them in the church and many people gathered, Stephen himself hurried off and went in to the emperor.
He raised an uproar before him too, crying out in distress and saying, “Christianity has perished! The ordinances of the Christians’ church have been destroyed!
All the ordinances and canons of the church of God have been thrown into confusion, trampled underfoot, and destroyed!
What is this lawless wickedness, that the priesthood of Orthodox Christians is being annulled by those who now hold power, and another is being conferred anew in its place?
For twenty years now, unworthy though I am, I have been a bishop, canonically ordained by the Orthodox at the command of Theodosius, patriarch of Alexandria.

And now that I have surrendered myself and placed myself in your hands, this man, acting wickedly as he has done to many others, wishes to strip me too of the priesthood of the Orthodox and ordain me anew in his own priesthood.
Let him show from which canons he learned this! Either he has no understanding or knowledge of the church’s canons,
or, even though he knows them, he transgresses them and tramples them underfoot in his arrogance, conceit, and error.
And if this order comes from you, and he does these things with your knowledge, let everyone know it. But you should know

that even behind your majesty's back he is trying to chase after accusations and pretexts drawn from the canons, and by this he is plotting to have you counted as a transgressor of the ecclesiastical laws.
And if it is with your knowledge and at your command that he annuls the priesthood and confers another anew, then command him
to annul baptism as well and baptize again, and only then to ordain priests anew.
For the nineteenth canon of the three hundred and eighteen fathers, concerning the destructive heresy of the followers of Paul of Samosata and others like him,
commands that they be baptized again, and that afterward those among them who are worthy should be ordained priests anew. This is because of the wickedness of their heresy.
Now, then, let this man first explain why he has come to this, and what prompted him, in his arrogance, to depose us and ordain us anew.”
When the emperor heard these things and realized that Stephen was bringing a just accusation and disputing with him on canonical grounds,
He was startled as if out of a deep sleep. He too went in and condemned this act, saying:
that it is truly wicked, unlawful, and contrary to the entire order of the church for priestly ordination to be annulled and performed anew.
It is shameful and utterly foreign to all the church’s regulations. He then commanded that this should never happen again in the church of God.
Immediately he also issued a formal decree, forbidding anyone to presume again to annul priestly ordination, except in cases of heresy specified by the canons.
If bishops were found doing this, they were to be deposed and sent into exile.
When this happened, and John learned that a strict command had been issued, he and his advisers devised a scheme to give a bribe,
so that the decree issued concerning this matter would be removed and never seen again.
Because of this, great hostility persisted between John and Stephen throughout their lives.
Then, with a cunning plan full of misleading deceit, as the outcome itself eventually revealed, John, together with all his advisers, sent men
and brought back those bishops whom he had sent into exile in monasteries and other places.
They deceived them by saying that they had brought them to discuss unity with them.
First, he sent for Paul the patriarch, took him from the monastery of the Acoemetae, and imprisoned him in his own episcopal residence.
He brought the others one after another and imprisoned them with him: namely, Paul, John, Stephen, and Elisha.
They had first devised a scheme and taken counsel together, and they sent them a document describing the union that had taken place between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch.
They sent word to them in their prison: “You must also unite with us in accordance with the union that took place between Cyril and John.”
When they received these things, considered them among themselves, and laughed at their trickery, they sent them this reply: “You have taken good counsel.
So, once we have acted and carried matters through as Cyril did, and have anathematized the Council of Chalcedon, expelled it, and cast it out of the church of God,
just as Cyril also did to the wicked Nestorius, we will not dispute with you about the remaining matters between us and you.
Instead, we will unite with you without hindrance. But if you do not approve of our doing what Cyril did, how, then, and in what way
do you propose to demand from us the union between him and John that came afterward, when Cyril’s earlier action has not been carried out?”
After this, John was being reproached by these bishops whom he had imprisoned in his episcopal residence,
in the debate concerning the faith, the corruption of the Council of Chalcedon, and the things done by it.
Every day they engaged him, having begun to accuse him firmly, dispute with him, and rebuke him forcefully.
They challenged him with questions, saying to him: “Show us, you who are great and hold the leadership of the church,
from what canon and ecclesiastical regulation you learned and received authority to annul the priestly ordination of orthodox bishops
and the other priests, whose years in the priesthood exceeded even those of your father, and to annul their ordination and ordain them anew into the priesthood of the two natures.”
Those who proclaim and teach a quaternity in place of the hidden and holy Trinity.

And in what ecclesiastical rule did you find this and commit yourself to it: to abolish the priesthood of the true orthodox and establish in its place, anew, another priesthood of adherents of the council?
"For what reason, or on what pretext, and as if from what heresy, as the canons prescribe,
did you receive and absolve these men, who because of the heresy of the two natures accuse you and flee from communion with you?"
and because of the blasphemies of the council and the Tome of Leo, which proclaim and teach a quaternity in place of the holy Trinity?
But you have absolutely no grounds to accuse and condemn them for heresy, and yet you depose them from their priesthood.
But if you do indeed have a case against those whom you unlawfully deposed from the priesthood, tell us now, and we will cease our judgment and accusation concerning these matters.
For if you, on your own, apart from all the orders and canons of the Church,
have authorized yourselves to use these measures, to depose true priests and ordain them anew, then it would have been consistent with this
to invalidate their baptism as well and baptize them anew, according to the force of the injunctions of the canons.
For see, that canon of the three hundred and eighteen concerning the corrupting heresy of the party of Paul of Samosata,
it commanded that they should first be baptized anew, and then that those found worthy should become priests anew.
And if you now suppose that you received as heretics those whom you forcibly led away as captives,
and ordained them priests anew, how is it that you fulfill the one requirement but have neglected the first?
John himself listened to all this in silence and knew that the accusations were justified, having no way out that he could use to answer them.
At last he answered, saying, “Since I see that you are troubled and offended over this matter of ordination—as indeed all these things
I heard from you while I remained silent—if this practice concerning ordination is corrected and abolished, will that satisfy you, and will you unite with us?”
But they said to him, “What correction can you make after all this wrongdoing and corruption and the unlawful deed you have committed?
For you did not do this only here and restrain the surge of your anger and hatred,
but you extended this lawbreaking even to other regions, in opposition to all the orders and all the ecclesiastical canons.
Either you did not know these, and so broke through them and went beyond them, trampled them and transgressed them,
or, knowing them, you despised them and acted insolently against them, and plunged into all this lawbreaking.
And do not let this be forgotten by you: at whatever time it may happen, whether during your lifetimes or if it happens after your death,
all these matters must come under thorough examination and canonical investigation, if the world continues and the church of God remains.
Then again, that other thing you did at the end deserves astonishment, to become a byword, and to be recounted with wringing of hands.
Whether this was done by you in an outburst of anger or hatred, through the arrogance of power, or with some other intention,
now judge for yourselves and consider whether you acted as duty required and with sound judgment.
that after you fell upon these people as if taking captives, and captured them as if in a raid, and subdued them and forced them into communion with you,
and after thirty-six consecrations and liturgies throughout the whole feast of Unleavened Bread, which they also celebrated with you after us,
having received them in their original priesthood and seated their priests with your own priests in the sanctuary throughout all the aforementioned days of the invocation,
and having also received the deacons in their existing diaconal order alongside the other deacons and established them in their rank,
you finally, after all this, senselessly let yourselves be drawn into some strange trickery to annul their original priesthood.
We now leave this to your own judgment and the examination of your conscience, so that you may consider why you should strip them of the priesthood and ordain them anew.
if indeed it pleases you this way, that you should act like this without order and without the ecclesiastical canons,
you should have done this before receiving them to celebrate the Eucharist with you,
did not all those who were with you turn back after these liturgies and enter into communion in their former priesthood?
turn around and depose them and ordain them anew.
After many things had been said on both sides—we pass over some of them because of their number and the length of an account of them—
the accused knew within himself that he was liable to blame and not free from accusation, if he examined what he had done.
This was especially true of his final actions in deposing those whom he had subsequently received into ministry, only to turn around and depose them.
For concerning these matters, his silence showed that he himself was at fault, although he used filthy and frivolous words against them in a disorderly manner.
For when the members of the synod saw that they had now failed in what they had contrived,
the victorious Emperor Justin proceeded to issue an edict, thinking that through it he would bring about unity.
After diligently drafting it, he immediately sent it to the bishops who were confined in the episcopal residence,
through a certain Zacharias, a sophist and chief physician of the palace, who was a native of Sura in Roman territory and had long been considered orthodox.
He was therefore sent to them by the emperor with the text of the edict they had drafted.
And he said to them: "This edict the merciful king has sent to you, which he has [?] on your account."
so that through it you too, together with everyone belonging to your party, may be united.
He has given you permission and has also commanded this: when you have read it, whatever you see in it that is deficient and needs correction,
you are to correct. And if anything useful to the right confession, which you wish to prevail, is missing, add it without fear.”
When the bishops received this decree, they took it and read it. They saw that it was incomplete, although it contained certain things that conflicted with the Council of Chalcedon.
Yet it also contained things drawn from that council and supporting it. Since they had been instructed to do so, they drew up articles, that is, corrections:
If their opponents had allowed these to be inserted into it, it would undoubtedly have brought about unity.
Then he took the emendations that he had, and brought them and showed them to John, his confidant and counsellor, and to the rest of their whole synod.
When they heard the corrections, they were alarmed and shaken, and great fear fell upon them.
For if these were adopted, they would uproot the entire heresy of the two natures.
Those thoroughgoing Nestorians were alarmed and disturbed even more than the semi-Nestorians. They stirred up trouble and caused an uproar throughout the church.
They went about agitating the clergy and the people, saying, “If these additions are adopted, the whole church will be thrown into confusion and ruined.”
Finally, they assembled their entire party and went in to the emperor to persuade him not to have these corrections inserted into his edict.
They also stirred up the people of the palace, many of whom were themselves unsound in their Christianity.
Especially so was the quaestor, whose name was Anastasius the Palestinian: besides being a pagan, he was also a Samaritan.
When they came before the emperor and these corrections were read to him, they pleased him, and he praised them highly. He ordered them to be inserted into the edict and written into the document.
Then all those who had entered—the clerics, the laymen, and the rest of the senate—raised an outcry against him, saying:
“My lord, if you put these articles into your edict and they are introduced into the church, it will immediately be overturned and ruined.
And while you want small things to come in and take hold, great things are going out of the Church.
As they clamored against him, he became angry and turned to face them, saying, “These articles are sound.
But I know that all of you are Nestorians, sick in your consciences, and that you take no pleasure in the orthodox faith.
If you do not keep quiet, I will release the bishops, bring them out, and unleash them against you.
They will fall upon you like wolves and tear you apart, and you will not be able to stand against them.” Then he gave the quaestor an order, saying:
“If you do not bring me twenty copies of the edict containing these corrections this very evening, I will take off your head.”
Then the whole party of the Nestorians and the semi-Nestorians was alarmed, and they buzzed like bees driven by smoke.
Nevertheless, they managed to plead with him and frighten him with the prospect of disorder in the church.
When they pressed him hard, he yielded to them and left the matter to their wishes. They allowed him to insert only a few minor points from these corrections.
They themselves, however, heretically added a statement of their own at the end of the edict: “The church’s customs shall be preserved for it.”
This referred to the council, so that they could continue proclaiming it as was their custom.
They planned and arranged this cunningly, so that there would be no unity and the wheel would turn against them, as it had against the Nestorians.
For after the edict had been written in [?], as the emperor had commanded, he immediately signed it and sent it to the bishops who were in the episcopal residence.
He sent them this message: “Look, we have brought about unity as you wished, and now we have sent you an edict.
From now on you have no reason to delay uniting with us. Indeed, it was also for your sake that I issued this edict.”
But when those bishops read the edict and saw that the corrections they had made were not in it, but only some excerpts from them,
inserted according to the wishes of those who had selected them, they disregarded it, because their opponents had confused and muddled it as they wished.
For fear of the emperor, they had not dared to remove from it the statements that opposed the two natures.

But they had contrived to insert their own statements into it as far as they could. Thus it appears to contend against the council, yet also to fight on its behalf, and statements taken from the council and belonging to it are evident in the edict.
Then those bishops gave an answer to those who were present, saying:
“If the cause of stumbling and turmoil for the whole church—that is, the Council of Chalcedon—is removed, the church has no need even of this edict.
But if that council continues to be proclaimed in the church, not even a thousand edicts like this, posted in every place and every region, will establish unity.
"And the breach is still where it was. For this document also appears to be written against the synod and to replace it, and two points in it are plain to anyone who reflects on it."
Every day John himself solemnly warned the bishops, along with those who were sent to them on the emperor’s behalf, saying:
“Look! It is you who are thwarting and disturbing the unity of God’s church.
For now it has come after fifty years, and you are pushing it away, preventing and obstructing it, and refusing to unite.”
But they would reply to them, saying: “How are we thwarting unity?
You do not touch it with even one of your fingers, except with empty words and cunning, so that people will see you and think
that you truly care about unity, while you arrange to direct against us all the blame that comes from everyone.
What sort of union, then, are you trying to bring about? Or how can you ask us to unite with you
while you hold to the council that has torn apart and troubled the whole church of God, proclaiming it and cherishing it?
If you truly care about bringing about unity, as you say,
remove the stumbling block and the cause of stumbling from the clear path of faith, and cast it out of God’s church.
Then not only we, but all the faithful, rejoicing and freed from stumbling, will unite with you.”
Along with these were many other such statements, which we cannot encompass even in a very thick stack of sheets:
the things said between them every day in the exchanges of debate about these matters.
These are things that, because of the abundance of words and the bulk of the writings, we leave out and pass over, so that they might be considered [?] by those who encounter them.
Now, before the time of this persecution and these trials, afflictions, and imprisonments inflicted by the persecutors:
Besides these things, those bishops were also being harshly reproached by the rest of the orthodox, who argued with them and said:
“Why do you persist like this in contention and stubbornness, instead of acting with discretion and making concessions, so that there may be unity in the church of God?
Instead, you remain so stiff-necked and contend against those who hold power.
You do not care that you are going to destroy us, our homes, our children, and our possessions.
What does it matter to you if we lose our livelihoods and become beggars?”
Thus, while these things had already been said to them by the orthodox in harsh reproaches, as they were distressed over their wealth,
And besides these, those from among the synodal party were also being called to witness by them every day: "Why are you bringing it to nothing, so that there may be no union?"
they fell into grief and bitter weeping by day and by night, sitting together, weeping and lamenting with sobs.
In voices of lamentation they said, “What are we to do now? Look, we are being reproached from both sides; accusations are brought against us, and we are blamed.
And now, here we are, imprisoned in distress, and we are not allowed to see any of our acquaintances.
And these things that are directed against us, they say especially to the great and notable men of our side:
They deceitfully tell everyone, and make them believe, that they are concerned for unity. And now all the blame for the failure of unity—
since everyone supposes their words to be true—they lay upon us. And now, here we are, caught between both sides.
As for surrendering ourselves and relying on the deceitful promises and false oaths of our opponents,
we know that there is no truth among them, and that they are not at all fit to have unity brought about through their hands. But if we continue to stand against them in contention,
look, we are condemned by both sides for all generations to come, as those who thwart and obstruct the unity of the church of God.
Moreover, they even lend an appearance of truth to these people’s deceitful promises and lying words,
as though they had been ready to bring about unity, but we had prevented unity in the church.”
Along with many other things like these, such words were spoken among them with sobbing tears for many days.
We testify before God to the truth of these things, since we were close at hand and eyewitnesses to them all.
For thirty-three days they remained sharply opposed to one another in this debate: those of the synod who held authority,
and those opposed to the synod, who had been imprisoned by them and were being bitterly oppressed. Whenever they were summoned,
they were released and came out of the prison, went to the patriarch’s council chamber, and sat and debated for as long as those in authority wished.
Whenever they were either defeated by them or chose to do so, those bishops would leave with their guards and go inside, where they were confined behind three lines of guards.
one of the episcopate and one of the [?], and that outer one of the [?].
Meanwhile, the people belonging to each of them, from everywhere—not only the clerics, monks, and the other freeborn people accompanying them,
but also all their servants—were confined in dark and miserable prisons throughout the bishop’s residence.
They were all kept under guard, and not only that: they were also stripped by the episcopal officers and the decanal officers, as though by bandits.
If they were wearing clothes, these were stripped off, even worn-out things that were of no use to them; whether shoes or belts,
or straps or prayer beads were found on any one of them, or anything else, they were stripped of everything.
Everything found on them was taken away, and they were thrown onto the ground, stripped and distressed, even for lack of food.
People were not allowed at all to see them or to bring anything either to them or to the bishops.
Instead of the promised unity, they and all those with them were suffering and enduring these evils, these afflictions and trials.
This was especially because they openly rebuked those who were tormenting them.
After all this, once again, the bishops were finally summoned and brought out of their prison. By now, a harsh and shameless stand had been taken against them,
by John himself, the head of the see, and, even more than by him, by those who were sent by the emperor and acted as his representatives.
saying: "How much longer will you go on casting down and destroying in this way the unity of the Church of God?"
which our lord the emperor and we are striving to bring about? Day after day you obstruct and cast aside this good thing.
Are you not openly showing everyone that it is you, and no one else, who are thwarting it?
So now, once and for all: either unite, or be exposed as the ones who disturb, disrupt, and thwart the unity of the church.”
But those bishops, who were in mourning and sorrow, said,
“If matters are judged justly and with sound reasoning, it is not we who are obstructing unity, but you.
While your hearts are filled with the filth of opposition and Chalcedonian division, you want to portray us as the ones causing obstruction,
although you yourselves have neither established nor displayed within yourselves even the shadow of unity.
Instead, you deceitfully demand that we unite with the whole Chalcedonian falsehood,
and you are not striving to bring about the true unity of the church justly and rightly.
"And now, as we said from the beginning: if you truly want unity, and are not eager to practise crafty deceit and wicked contentiousness,
first remove the cause of division from among us, and there unity will stand in its place. Do not deceitfully use us as your excuse.”
And now, even though this has not entered your minds at all, why do you wrong and oppress us every day, adding pain to our torments
and to the distress of imprisonment and the other afflictions that we endure at your hands, without any fear of God on your part? Every day you torment us with your words,
and you drive a thorn into our sores. You do not fear God, although you see that our lives are already spent
and have wasted away and come to an end because of the afflictions surrounding us on every side. If you really intend to bring about unity, in keeping with your outward words,
reject the Council of Chalcedon, for it has disturbed, divided, and split the church,
as even you cannot deny. In this way undivided unity will be established throughout the church of God.
Again John and those with him say: “You yourselves are preventing this very thing—the rejection of the council, as you request.
For if you unite, the council too will immediately be rejected, and there will be complete unity.”
The bishops say: “It appears to us that you are trying to make us unite with your council.
Let this not mislead you or anyone else: until the breath leaves the nostrils of each of us,
the condemnation of the council and the Tome of Leo, which together divide our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ into two natures after the union, will not cease from our mouths.”
John and those with him say: “As we have told you many times, we and our lords the emperors
give you our word and oaths before God that, as soon as you unite, the council will be annulled,
and whatever comes out of our lips will not be changed." The bishops say: "If, then, you are ready to do this in accordance with your oaths,
why, then, do you not do it immediately, so that not only we but everyone may unite without any obstacle?
Instead, you want to deceive us by trickery and have us unite with the heresies of the two natures,
and afterward turn around and mock us. If this is what you think, you are mocking and deceiving yourselves.
For we know that your intentions and thoughts are not directed toward unity.
For you do not even appear to be speaking the truth, although in words you have offered to act, so that everyone may think that we have obstructed unity,
and so that we may be condemned by you and everyone else as those who obstruct it. For we are even sacrificing our lives for unity:
since we are relying on your words and promises, then as something already anathematized and cast out, the synod
while we enter into communion with you without its anathema ceasing from our mouth, whether perhaps once, or if it should happen twice.
But a third time, before the council has been condemned and rejected, we will have no share or communion with you forever and ever.
But we know that you will not make good on your words. And so that it may be revealed and made known to everyone that you have not prepared to bring about unity,
but think that you can deceive us and everyone else, here and now we commit ourselves to union with you, perhaps as many as two times.”
These things, along with many others without end, were spoken and testified between them.

And so those bishops yielded, saying, “Because of the oppression inflicted on us by the members of the synod, we now surrender ourselves, so that it may be known that we are not the ones obstructing matters.”
For everyone on both sides was speaking abusively of them, saying, “Look, the emperors and the patriarch are concerned and working hard and preparing to bring about unity,
but these prisoners are preventing and hindering them.” Thus, because of all these things, they surrendered themselves in great distress.
While loudly pronouncing anathema on the Council of Chalcedon, they were twice forced into communion with them,
As they agreed and were persuaded, from then on the anathema and rejection of the synod [were expected] from those who, by the decision of many oaths,
throughout all those thirty-three days, insistently demanding this from the emperor and the patriarch.
When these men began to go back on their words and put them off with excuses, saying, “We are writing to the pope of Rome, and if he agrees,
then we will reject the council. For we cannot break with Rome for your sake,” they answered them, saying,
“Now it is time for us too to repeat the words of the prophet Jonah: ‘Was this not what I said while I was still in my own country?’” And so it became known and clear to everyone
that those who were imprisoned and enduring bitter afflictions were not the ones preventing unity. Rather, they had even surrendered themselves for its sake.
Instead, it was those who held power and oppressed them, who lied in the promises and oaths they made to them,
wanting to lay all the blame—not only for their own contemporaries but also for the generations coming after them—on the bishops,
as the one which they had troubled and the unity of the Church of God which they had destroyed; if these men had not sacrificed their own lives for it, even though it was betrayed by them.
For who could adequately write or tell of the distress, mourning, lamentation, and heartbreak
that overtook those who had fallen into communion with the men who had plotted against them and ensnared them, although they had never been ensnared before?
They were now utterly ruined and spent. Their eyes were clouded and dim from weeping and lamenting before one another night and day.
The mourning of a woman for the husband of her youth is only a small illustration when compared with their mourning.
They had now even stopped eating their usual food. They continued without nourishment or consolation, and their tears neither ceased nor paused.
Each of them [?] covered his face, and they sat lamenting before one another in choking, bitter voices, now mourning all the more over themselves,
because, after all these struggles, imprisonments, and afflictions, they had thus been caught by deceitful trickery, brought low, and made to fall,
while unity still lay before them and had not been put into effect as promised.
So those who had deceived them, seeing that they were already ruined and wasting away toward destruction,
said to them, “Why are you killing your souls along with your bodies like this, as though you had sacrificed to idols?
Why, then, have you passed sentence on yourselves and persisted in all this weeping and lamentation, continually choking yourselves?”
“Take food and be comforted. Live, and do not die.” Despite the many such things said by their opponents, they continued without consolation.
And so they sat in mourning and weeping all the more, remaining bitterly distressed for many days, even after they had been released from prison and had come out.
Then they rallied and stood firm courageously. From then on they rebuked them and disputed with them even more openly, denouncing them as liars and deceivers.
And so they were again subjected to imprisonment and tortures harsher than the earlier ones.
Afterward, each one of them was sent to a different place of exile amid bitter suffering.
When the emperors learned of all this intense mourning and bitter sorrow, they sent for the bishops, brought them to the palace, and tried to comfort them, saying:
“Why have you fallen into all this distress of mourning, to the point of becoming so weak and like dead men? Take courage and be comforted.
For we trust in God that we will satisfy you and bring you together in complete unity. Do not be distressed.”
And when they reproached him at length about the things that had been spoken between them, and had proved false, and had not come to fulfilment, he said to them:
“Since we are preparing to go to the hot baths, wait for me twenty or thirty days. Know that we will return promptly for your sake.
We are preparing to speak about this very matter and to satisfy you, so that the whole church may be one and we may all rejoice.”
And so they were dismissed by him, after addressing many rebukes to him.
After thirty days, the emperor returned from the hot baths as he had promised.
While he had not yet entered the city but was still on the other side, at Chalcedon, John took his counselors and went out to meet him.
As became apparent again, he added accusations against those who had been imprisoned, saying, “These men have cut themselves off from us
and have turned away from the church altogether.” Then they took counsel about how to accomplish their purpose and deceive them again.
They drew up a list of the great cities and sent it to them through the quaestor, sending them this message:
“Since it is our responsibility to satisfy you, and we are concerned for your honor and wish to make [?] for you,
we have now sent you this list of well-known cities, without ourselves specifying in which city each of you should be.
Instead, we have left this to your own choice, so that each of you may choose for himself whichever city pleases him.”
When the illustrious quaestor took the list and entered the city, he sent for the bishops so that he could give them the list. All these things,
along with many others, he said to them on behalf of the emperor. But they did not look at the list and were unwilling to accept it from him.
They said, “Tell the victorious emperor: ‘We are not sacrificing ourselves in order to become bishops in cities,
but because of our hope in the promises of unity. For we are bishops, even though we are unworthy.
"But if the promises of unity are fulfilled for us, and the oaths that were made among us over a period of many days..."
And we, because of these things, and so that the accusations against us—that we were supposedly destroying unity—might not be substantiated,
we gave ourselves over to communion with those who meant to deceive, and they thought that they had deceived us.
They did not know that they had led themselves astray, not us. And now, if the council is not set aside and unity established in accordance with the promises and oaths,
God forbid that we should ever again have communion with those who mention its name, forever and ever.
When they had thus made their firm decision and refused to accept, the quaestor became angry and went and reported these things to the emperor.
He too became angry and was stirred to great fury. He threatened them and made harsh threats, which he eventually carried out.
Then, filled with fury, the emperor sent for the patriarch of the city and confronted him harshly, with grievous insults,
while he said: "You," he said, "turned the bishops round, those who with much toil had at last agreed to enter into communion with us; and you, behold, have turned them away from us."
In this agitated state, he ordered the senate to enter the bishop’s residence and have the matters that had arisen between them adjudicated,
with the patriarch himself also standing trial. If they proved him wrong, he too was to be condemned.
Accordingly, on the following day, members of the senate entered the bishop’s residence with the quaestor, as ordered, and the bishops were summoned for judgment.
They were required, ostensibly by command, to remain in communion with the adherents of the council, keeping quiet and demanding nothing further.
But they stood firm and fought the contest vigorously and courageously, openly and fearlessly denouncing
all the deceitful promises, all the oaths that had been broken, the truth that had been wronged and trampled underfoot, and the other things of this kind.
Along with this, they openly addressed the senate with great boldness, pronouncing an anathema against the entire heresy of the two natures.
They spoke firmly at the beginning, in the middle, and also at the end, and once again they decisively and finally broke off communion with them forever.
There were also the many other things done and said there in that contest of courageous struggle.
Eventually the anger of the senators and the patriarch blazed up against the bishops,
and they ordered that they be dragged out of their presence, separated from one another, and sent into exile.
This was quickly carried out. They were taken out and separated, and never saw one another again. They were sent into exile,
some to monasteries, some to islands in the sea, and some to cramped and miserable places of confinement in hospices.
when it was decreed against them that they be imprisoned, and that no one, either of their own people or of others, be allowed to see any one of them.
and many other things that were decreed against them cruelly, harshly and pitilessly, with bitter weight and bonds of iniquity, as though against murderers.
Perhaps, however, all these things that have been said and written may seem to those versed in lofty learning and sharp in understanding, who scrutinize these words closely,
to have been said and written by the writer as embellishments, employed by him in the manner of literary composition.
as the one by whose will in [these] matters these things were written, as if by him. Otherwise, from where [would they come] in such orderly fashion,
how to recount and write down all these things that happened and were said between the two sides, and to hand them all down in writing?
Moreover, as is apparent, in his account he is aligned with one side, rebukes the other side, and fights on behalf of one side.
But now let those who hold this opinion understand this: the writer of all these things was not outside the struggle,
and he was not far from the struggle; he would receive these things by report from afar and from others,
and then writing them down and handing them down in his book. Rather, he himself was one of those engaged in the struggle.
In the great conflict, together with the others—or even more than they—he courageously bore sufferings and endured the afflictions of persecution and imprisonment.

He and the others spoke and debated before the emperor and the patriarch, not only about these brief recollections that he handed down in this book, but also about a hundred times as many other matters.
Because of the great length of the history and the limitless mass of words, he passed over most of these and used only a few of them.
Moreover, although he belonged to the side opposed to the two natures and was arrayed against them, as his account itself makes clear,
he nevertheless observed the proper manner of historical writing, without partiality or mistreatment and injustice toward the opposing side,
as though to strengthen his own side. Rather, as at the beginning of this book of his history—or as he had previously said and promised—
he became an advocate for the truth and preserved the true character of both sides concerning the things that were said, put forward, and debated,
even though he used only a few of them, since he could not bring into the written record even one hundredth of what was said and done.
At that same time Conon was also arrested, the head of the heresy of those who dare to count natures, substances, divinities, and gods in the holy and consubstantial Trinity.
He too was arrested and imprisoned for a time in the bishop’s residence, together with the others. They demanded that he make a written declaration, as a heretic.
He disputed this and did not do it. When the victorious emperor learned of this, he swore by the Mother of God, saying,
“Even if he petitions and enters the church and receives communion without making a written declaration of repentance, I will not enter it or receive communion in it.”

And so, because he was a heretic and a blasphemer, when Photius, the son of Belisarius’s wife, came to the imperial city at that time, Conon was handed over to him, and he took him along to Palestine.
He imprisoned him in the monastery called the New Monastery. He remained there for three years. Then he was released and went to the region of Cilicia.
This Photius was the son of the wife of Belisarius the patrician, whose name was Antonina.
He had been in military service and had gone on campaigns with Belisarius. Eventually, for some reason, he went and had his hair cut and put on the monastic habit,
though he did not undertake the monastic way of life at all. Rather, he wore the habit of a monk under an assumed name.
After a short time, unable to subdue his unruliness through the fear of God, he hurried to the emperor.
While outwardly clothed in the monastic robe, he was sent to the regions of Syria because of the Samaritans who had rebelled.
And while he wanted to please people, he angered God his Maker, as he too pursued filthy profits under various pretexts.
He threw himself into plundering, robbery, and oppression of people, and into uprooting and destruction,
so that, as though fleeing barbarian captors, the great and small throughout all the regions of the East,
so that even the bishops and clergy of all the cities would flee from before him. But also everyone who was...
whether in a city or in the countryside, whom he learned had daily bread to spare, he would seize, plunder, imprison, hang up, and torture.
He imposed assessments of pounds of gold on them—on anyone at all, whether he possessed anything or not.
Even if someone sold himself, his children, his house, and his possessions, there was no way for anyone to reverse the word he had spoken.
For whenever he seized someone, he would say, “Give [?] pounds, because the emperor needs gold to spend on the wars.”
In this way he collected hundred-pound sums and sent them off, so that through this he would be given authority to do whatever he wished to whomever he wished,
and people would not stand against him. For he likewise demanded large payments from the bishops as well.
If anyone resisted him, he was immediately, without delay, hoisted up on a rope, either behind his head, by his shoulder blades, or by one arm.
Thus, as is reported, he imposed an assessment of three hundred pounds on the bishop of Ashkelon.
When the bishop wailed and solemnly swore that he did not have it, he gave orders, and the bishop was hung up on a rope. He left him hanging and went away,
ordering that, even if he remained hanging for three days, he was not to be taken down until the hundred-pound sums arrived.
And so he was not taken down from the rope until the three hundred pounds arrived.
He did the same to many others, until the land trembled before him, as did all the magistrates, governors, and other authorities.
When many people complained before the emperor, the emperor wrote to him, “It is a sin
for you to send us the proceeds of plunder.” But he wrote back to him, “My lord, do not fear sin on account of the gold I send.
"This sin be on my head." With him there was a band of monks who were suited for these things,
and also of spatharii [?] and of mastigai [?] and of asphetarii [?], and also an army of Romans.
Thus, after living in this foul manner of destruction, deceit, and brutality, entirely without any fear of God,
for a full twelve years, his end overtook him, and he received his disgrace, with an evil end and a cursed memory.
After him another man arose, named Abraham, the abbot of the monastery in Jerusalem called the New Monastery.
So in the middle of the persecution a letter was written and sent to Alexandria, and sophists, scholastics and ship-owners came up, and many others besides.
The secret intention was to require them to attend a council, but the outward appearance was that it was for the sake of unity.
Thus they also employed both methods against them in practice, when they were finally being required to receive communion.
But they courageously resisted and disputed for many days, for about a year, without yielding or giving in at all.
Finally, some of them were released, because the authorities were afraid to compel them, on account of the shipments of wheat sent from there to the imperial capital.
Some of them were detained for as long as three years, but nothing came of it. And so they were all released.
After this, a report was written to the emperor that the orthodox bishops had appointed successors to the blessed Theodosius:
not just one bishop, but two. He became extremely angry and ordered all the heads of the clergy to be arrested and sent to him.
This was done. They were arrested and taken up, and remained there until after the death of John the patriarch.
And then it was Awṭok [?], who was before him. And he came in after his death and released them, after one year.
Again, many times they were sent to Egypt, and many monks were summoned and came, those who were believed to know hidden things,
and to discern the future—so that they might reveal how many years the emperor and empress would live, what was going to happen during his reign, and other things of this kind.
Thus some of them, when pressed about these matters, were questioned while admitting that they knew nothing.
Instead, they spoke about moral instruction, justice, and righteousness: when these things are practiced, they please God and bring people close to him.
Consequently, these men were not accepted, because they would not stoop to giving a pleasing answer as they had been asked.
They were immediately dismissed and driven out of the city to return to their own country.
Others, however, seeking to please people, gave way to the weakness of that pretense, which was eventually exposed.
These men were retained with honor and spent a long time enjoying comforts and gifts of food. Such things happened many times.
For when all the monasteries mentioned above were led away violently and lawlessly,
a few of their members received communion, while the rest were cast into other convents. Those clerics were installed everywhere,
so that in each convent they would offer the Eucharist and give communion to those who complied. The name of the council was written down and proclaimed in them.
John took down the images of all the orthodox fathers and installed his own images everywhere. For these deeds God repaid him according to what he had done.
For after his bitter and agonizing death, and the accession of Eutychius, who had been his predecessor and returned to office after his death,
his images were removed, and images of Eutychius were installed in their place in the churches.
And all these convents of women, for the most part, returned and became orthodox. In some of them, however, a few young girls remained,
and others were entering every day who received communion in accordance with the council. They wore the monastic habit and received communion from the clerics.
But these women openly broke away, and not one of them continued to receive communion, especially after John's death.
Now, before John’s death, while he was drunk with furious zeal for persecuting Christians,
and thirsted like a wolf for the blood of lambs, he would go in to the peaceable and gentle Caesar Tiberius,
eager to inflame him too with furious zeal like his own. After saying many things to him against the faithful, he asked him:
“I want you to answer me truthfully about what I ask you. Are these people whom you are urging me to persecute pagans?”
He could not lie, however, and said to him, “They are not pagans.”
He said to him, “Then are they heretics?” He answered him, “Nor are they heretics, my lord.”
He said to him, “Then, according to your own testimony about them, they are Christians.” He answered again, “Christians they certainly are.”
He said to him, “If, according to your testimony, they are Christians, how can you urge me to become a persecutor of Christians,
like Diocletian and the rest of the pagan kings. "Go, sit in your church and be quiet, and do not trouble us any more with these things."
Thus the violence of his savagery was checked until wrath from heaven overtook him, as we related above, and he departed from this earthly life.
After this, again as we related above, when Eutychius came in and those clerics who were accustomed to plunder and robbery began to inflame him,
he too set out and went in to the gentle Caesar Tiberius Constantine, saying many things to him against the whole body of the faithful. But he too answered him:
“The wars with the barbarians, who surround us on every side, are enough for us. We cannot also stir up another war against Christians.
Go, stay where you are, and be quiet. If you can persuade them through discussion or admonition, do so; but if not, leave them alone.
Do not persecute them, and do not trouble us, for we are beset by the trials of wars on every side.” Thus he too restrained himself for the time being and kept quiet.
Now all those congregations of the orthodox that John of Sirimis had uprooted and shut down,
when God had sent upon him the chastisement of harsh wrath from heaven, they all began to [?] and to open to them.
At first they did so fearfully, quietly, and little by little. Even while he was still alive, they gained new members and grew,
especially when he had been struck by the blow of wrath and his mind had now become clouded by the fire of death that had seized his heart and was blazing in his bowels.
So, in the end, those who shared his wishes and served his wickedness, knowing what he wanted, would go in and say to him, “Look, these enemies of the church and the synod
have opened their meeting places again and have spread more widely than before. They rejoice in your illness and pray for your death.
If you command us, we will torment them more than before and make them suffer harm.”
But he would angrily rebuke them in a loud voice, saying, “Get away from me, you murderers!
Have your fill of my humiliation! It is you, more than anyone, who have brought me to this humiliation and misery,
"Enough of the curses, which stir up the wrath from heaven and bring it upon me."
“Leave my presence, and let no one bring this matter before me again.” And so they left him, bowing their heads.
Both before his death, as we said, and again after his death.
which happened soon afterward, they now gathered in the believers’ meeting places quite openly, without fear.
Now this monastery of Cathara was built by Narses while he was the emperor’s record keeper in the palace, before he went to Rome,
As one who was preparing to leave the palace and go to have his head tonsured and live there, he settled monks in it who had been persecuted from Cappadocia,
while he bought not a few villages for it, built a remarkable church in it, made a guesthouse in it, and acquired not a few revenues for it.
And so he was sent to Rome, where, through the help of God, who accompanied him, he distinguished himself with great victories in many battles.
There, in those regions, he departed this world. His bones were brought back and deposited in the monastery; the emperors brought him, laid him there, and honored him as a saint.
After John, who had been a patrician in the imperial city and had been sent there, had completed [?] years as bishop of Alexandria and died,
a man named Eulogius, a guesthouse administrator from Antioch, was appointed after him. He became pope there in the third year of the victorious Tiberius.
As for the party of the Julianists, there was Dorotheus, who had been appointed many years before and held office there.
As for the party of Theodosius, after his death there was first a man named Theodore, a Syrian administrator.
When the clergy and the rest learned of this, they turned against him. Since they would not accept him without canonical procedure, they took action and appointed another over him, named Peter.
After this man had served and ordained more than eighty bishops, he died. They appointed a Syrian named Damian, and they remained divided.
Now in Antioch the Great in Syria, in the days of Emperor Anastasius, there was Flavian.
He was accused of the heresy of the two natures and was expelled from his see, after serving for [?] years. After him came Severus the Orthodox.
He held office for six years. At the beginning of the reign of the elder Justin, the first of that name, he left his see.
And after the years that he spent in the desert of Egypt, he died there. And while Antioch was without a bishop for one year,
Paul the Jew finally came down. He had been the custodian of the shrine of the blessed Euphemia in Chalcedon.
This man brought the diptych in which the synod was inscribed down to the East.
After he had held office for about two years, it became known that he was a Nestorian. He too was expelled and left.
After him came Euphrasius, the son of Samaritans. In his seventh year Antioch was overthrown by an earthquake, and he died in it.
After him, in turn, came Ephraim of Amida, son of Appian, a wicked persecutor worse than Paul and Euphrasius.
And he lived for some years and died. And after him there was Domninus the Roman, [?]. And after him there was Anastasius.
who had been apocrisiarius of Alexandria.
And because of this, Justin the Younger brought charges against him and expelled him. In his place a man was sent, the head of the monastery of Mount Sinai, whose name was Gregory.
And again, after a long time, those who were opposed to the synod of Chalcedon made Sergius the first [successor] in place of Severus.
He was a man from Tella by origin. After completing about three years, he died in the imperial city, where he was living.

Then, after some further time, he was succeeded by a certain Paul, an Alexandrian, the personal attendant of Theodosius of Alexandria. He had come to office at his command and with his knowledge in those evil days.
Through the schism that arose between this man and the blessed Jacob, the church of the faithful was divided and became two factions.
The two sides fell into unrelenting battles and conflicts with one another. And those opposed to Paul, in turn,
after Jacob’s death, unlawfully appointed another patriarch in Antioch, a man named Peter, from the city of Callinicum.
These events, briefly stated, continued in this way down to the present time, when these things are being written, which is the year eight hundred and ninety-two.
In Constantinople, after Epiphanius, Anthimus was brought to the episcopate.
This man had formerly been bishop of the city of Trebizond, and he was summoned to the royal city.
After he had been there for some years, when Severus of Antioch had been summoned from Egypt by Justinian’s command
to discuss unity, Anthimus learned through Severus’s teaching about the transgression and perversity of the Council of Chalcedon
and about Leo’s blasphemies in his Tome. He abandoned the throne of the imperial city, departed, and joined Severus and Theodosius of Alexandria.
After him, a certain Menas, an Alexandrian who had been the administrator of Samson’s hospice, occupied the throne of the imperial city.
After completing some years, he departed from this world. He was succeeded by a young monk named Eutychius, the representative of Amasia.
After holding office for about twelve years, he was deposed and removed from his see. John succeeded him.
He was a Syrian from the village of Sarmin in the territory of Antioch. When he took office, he deposed Eutychius, and Eutychius deposed him.
And when John had completed twelve and a half years, he died. And Eutychius was summoned again and returned to his see.
The first book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished. It contains forty-two chapters.
Next, the second book of the Ecclesiastical History, containing fifty-two chapters, which are as follows.
First chapter: about how the bishops, when they saw that they had been deceived and mocked, broke off communion with the Synodites.
Second: about Paul the patriarch, and about the written statement that he made and by which he was trapped.
Third: about Stephen, bishop of Cyprus, and about the summoning of Paul.
Fourth: about John, who was over the pagans.
Fifth: about the afflictions and trials that came upon John.
Sixth: about a vision that appeared to John many times. [?]
Seventh: about the exile of John.
Eighth: about Paul's flight from the episcopal palace.
Ninth: about the illustrious Andrew, the queen's sacellarius, and about the struggles in which he contended.
Tenth: about Queen Sophia, who used to take communion with the Orthodox until two years before she became queen.
Eleventh: about three men of consular rank who were also steadfast, and who stood firm and contended valiantly.
Twelfth: about two noblewomen who were also steadfast and contended firmly.
Thirteenth: about Sergius and Sergius, our presbyters, and about the scourgings and imprisonments they endured.
Fourteenth: about Andrew, the imprisoned presbyter.
Fifteenth: about the deaconess of those who wash the poor and the sick.
Sixteenth: about another great deaconess.
Seventeenth: about how from that time on persecutions were stirred up in every place.
Eighteenth: concerning the things that were told about the Catholicos of Dvin, the great city of Persian Armenia, and about those who were with him.
Nineteenth: concerning the things that were said and done before their king by the Magians, the magnates of the Persian kingdom.
Twentieth: concerning the beginning of the hostility of Chosroes, king of the Persians, against Christianity.
Twenty-first: concerning the things that were afterwards done by Chosroes in Persian Armenia.
Twenty-second: concerning the things that were told about the Catholicos and those who were with him, and the rest.
Twenty-third: concerning how, when the Armenian bishops came, they entered in simplicity and received communion.
Twenty-fourth: concerning the things that were done in the end, when the Armenians gave in.
Twenty-fifth: concerning the fearful chastisement and harshness that overtook John.
Twenty-sixth: concerning the humiliation and the torment of just judgement that overtook John the Sirmian, together with his being persecuted by a demon.
Twenty-seventh: concerning how this John tore out and took down all the images of the Orthodox.
Twenty-eighth: concerning Theodulus, the persecuting deacon.
Twenty-ninth: concerning the king's quaestor.
Thirtieth: concerning how, when the churches of the Orthodox were united through persecution.
Thirty-first: concerning the summoning and the entry of Eutychius.
Thirty-second: concerning the things that were said by the archdeacon of Rome.
Thirty-third: concerning how, when Eutychius was summoned.
Thirty-fourth: concerning the images of John that Eutychius took down.
Thirty-fifth: concerning the book on the quaternity, that is, on the two natures, which Eutychius composed.
Thirty-sixth: concerning how Eutychius turned to the heresy of those who deny the resurrection of bodies.
Thirty-seventh: concerning how, when Eutychius was being grumbled against by everyone.
Thirty-eighth: concerning the [?] made by Andrew the sacellarius.
Thirty-ninth: concerning a certain sister, a nun.
Fortieth: concerning the responsory of Thursday of the Mysteries, which Eu[?] (probably Eutychius) wanted to change.
Forty-first: concerning the things that again befell John, who was called 'over the pagans', in the end, after all his trials.
Forty-second: concerning Paul.
[Chapter] forty-three: about Liberius.
[Chapter] forty-four: about Eutris [?], who came after Paul.
[Chapter] forty-five: about the Condobaudites.
[Chapter] forty-six: about the Cappadocian monks.
[Chapter] forty-seven: about the tangled orthodoxy.
[Chapter] forty-eight: about the elephants.
[Chapter] forty-nine: about the fire.
