they finally began throwing it into the fire and burning it. All these evils continued without restraint, until no congregation could be found meeting openly anywhere in the city.
The cause of all these evils was a certain Pharbina, a slave of Andrew.
When the persecution began, Andrew, who was the empress’s treasurer, left the palace and his service and departed for the sake of the true faith.
And he was plundered and confined in the monastery of Dalmatius, and he was not released. This man had a barbarian slave whom he had raised and zealously taught letters.
He had been trusted throughout his household, but in the end he rebelled against him and went and surrendered himself to Eutychius.
And he appointed him to be informer and [?] against all the priests and all the clergy.
Thus, to his master’s hurt, he would lead church advocates, excubitors, Romans, and clerics,
and go and drag everyone away, taking them off and putting them in prison after they had been barbarously plundered.
They carried off and took everything they had, even taking large amounts of gold from many of them.
Even if someone had gone in and hidden in a hole, so to speak, this man would cunningly make his way in and seize him,
rob him, and imprison him. This man became a trial and an adversary to all the priests, all the congregations, and all the faithful in the imperial city,
including us along with the rest. The evils this man inflicted on the whole church of the faithful are beyond telling and without end.
Now these sisters were sisters by birth. While they were still little girls, their mother died.
And their father placed them in a monastery. And he too died, and he left to them, that is, to their monastery, everything he owned.
As time passed, they grew up and reached maturity. Then the persecution under John overtook them, and afterward the persecution under Eutychius.
When they were forcing the whole convent to receive Communion from them, they seized some of the women and distributed them among the convents in the city.
But these two sisters stood firm as diamond, especially the elder.
They subjected her to every kind of torture and every affliction of harsh imprisonment, hunger, and thirst.
But she grew ever stronger, more radiant, and more fervent in faith. She rebuked and reproached all the women in whose convent she was imprisoned,
saying, “You, all your priests, and everyone who shares your views are strangers to the Holy Trinity.”
As people who uphold a quaternity in its place, you also side with the Council of Chalcedon,
which condemns Nestorius in appearance, but in practice and in truth holds to his faith and confesses two natures, just as he does.
And you side with it, along with everyone who agrees with it.” Thus she defeated them all, and they went in to complain to the bishop, crying out:
“Unless you order this trial to be taken away from us, you should know that we will all leave our convent.
For we cannot endure her insults, her abuse, and her arguing.” So he sent word to the exarch of the convents to send for her, judge her, and have her tortured,
and to take her out and put her in another convent, stricter than that one. The women there were to be ordered to torment her until they brought her into submission.
How, when the exarch's officer went to her and they began to accuse and threaten her, she laughed at them with authority.
mocking them and saying, “What is this, you pagans and murderers? Are you threatening me, a weak woman? If you have come only to threaten,
and do not kill, as is your custom and that of the man who sent you, you are not men, and I do not even count you among the living.”
So while they angrily beat her with a staff as though she were a camel, she mocked them still more,
condemning them and calling out to them, “You pagans, persecutors and murderers of Christians!” She challenged them to kill her,
saying, “You are pagans, not Christians! For Christians do not persecute Christians.
But you show yourselves to be pagans, and you display the deeds of your paganism.”
So when these men too were defeated by her, they dragged her away and imprisoned her in another convent, ordering the women there to torment her harshly.
How, after she had spent a few days there, these also began to cry out and flee from her.
They put her in many convents in this way, but could not overcome her strength.
And he ordered Eutyches: "Bring her here to the church." And when the people of the exarch's household heard this, they went in and said to Eutyches:
“You should know, my lord, that if she comes to you, unless you cut out her tongue or take off her head, there is no insult or mockery she will leave unsaid to your face.
And when she is beaten and flogged, she only does it all the more, ready to be killed and eager for death.”
Finally, when they brought her into the church, many people took turns confronting her and heaped intimidation and threats upon her. She mocked them all as though they were lifeless corpses,
and rebuked them at length, until they were all defeated by her on every count. Finally they released her to return to her convent.
Thus she brought relief to her whole convent, for they no longer put pressure on its women. Shuddering at her struggles, they said,
“If one sister from that convent stood firm through all these struggles without weakening, who could withstand their strength when they all stand together?”
Now the mighty Eutychius, as in his other dealings, arrogantly [?], intending to show himself a teacher,
and schemed to abolish and put an end to the established practices of the church services that had existed from the beginning, and to establish and confirm his own destruction:
He was the one who wrote it out on notices on the Thursday of the Mysteries, sent it to all the churches, and ordered that, once the anthem used from the beginning was abolished,
his own should be used, threatening and intimidating those who dared to use the original one and abandon his.
As a result, not only the clergy of all the churches and of the monasteries for men and women were disturbed and troubled by this, but also the whole city and the entire senate.
It nearly came to a great uprising against him, not only from the churches and monasteries, but also from the whole city.
These matters were even brought to the emperor’s attention by some members of the senate.
But when the bishop hurried in to the emperor in a fit of anger to complain to him about these things,
the emperor rebuked him severely, saying, “How long will you refuse to control yourself and remain quiet?
Look, you have disturbed and troubled the whole city! How can you change their ancient customs?
And take care that they do not stone you!” He said to him, “My lord, I composed one of my own that is far more suitable than the original.”
The emperor said to him, “You should know that even if you had brought your anthem down from heaven, they would not accept it at all.
Go, remain in your church, and follow what was established in it by the early fathers.” Thus he restrained his impetuosity, and his threats ceased and fell silent.
Now this John, who was called “the one over the pagans” and was bishop of Ephesus, after all the trials, imprisonments, persecutions, and exiles he had endured,
Finally he was pressed to hand over the deed of an estate that had been given to him by Callinicus, the king's praepositus and patrician:
When John received it, he spent a great deal on it and renovated it. He built a church on it, made three cisterns there, and designated it a monastery.
When persecution arose from John, he took away from him the place he had designated a monastery, installed adherents of the council there, and sent him into exile on an island in the sea.
When John died and Eutychius took office, he demanded that he hand over his deed of gift for the estate and the rest of his documents relating to the estate.
And not only that, but also the church furnishings, books, and other possessions. After many days of persecution and oppression,
he seized him and put him in prison, demanding and taking from him all the documents for the estate.
While he was imprisoned, he assembled against him the whole company of church legal officers and laymen, who brought proceedings against him over the church furnishings and the other things.
But he was strengthened by grace and said to them, “What church furnishings and what possessions are you demanding?
"As for these things that you gave there, whether you or others: it is the one who gave me the ministry who should come and demand them from me."
For look, you have unjustly and forcibly taken all the title deeds for the estate that I possessed, without any fear of God.
Read them and see. Is the name ‘monastery’ in them? Is it written in them that I received church furnishings? Yet that is what is being demanded of me.
For I acted unwisely when I designated it a monastery. Otherwise, it was not a monastery at all.”
Thus, with God’s help, he refuted them, and they all left him alone concerning these matters. But they demanded and took five loaves from him.
for they had been bought for her for three hundred [?], with the claim: "I bought these in the name of the monastery."
While he was in prison, he provided a surety, and then he was released and escaped the distress of imprisonment.
Paul’s story, then, deserves great sorrow. He was a sincere, quiet, humble, and innocent man,
and, like Jacob, he had long lived in the tent of his monastery in the village district.

When John of Sirimis learned about him, he immediately sent to Asia. He had him brought in, bound and fettered with iron chains, and imprisoned him under harsh conditions in his own episcopal residence.
Through those bonds and many torments, he forced him to submit to him and receive communion from him.
Out of shame before the man’s gray hair and dignity, however, he did not reveal the deceit in his heart or what he had plotted against him.
But after he had subdued him and shown that he was pleased with him, he sent him on to the bishop of Aphrodisias. And he wrote
to him: “Depose this man from his episcopate and ordain him anew. Appoint him in the city of Antioch, which is under your authority.”
As soon as that bishop received Paul and the letters, he seized him, while Paul remained unaware of their deceit.
He said to him, “The patriarch has ordered me to depose you from your episcopate and ordain you anew.”
When he heard this, he began to wail and said, “You people! You are pagans!
I was ordained many years ago and have been a bishop ever since. I was ordained by three bishops, in accordance with the canonical order.
Why, then, am I now being deposed contrary to the canons and wickedly ordained anew?
If you are annulling my priesthood and ordaining me anew, then first annul my baptism too, and baptize me anew!”
They were not persuaded, but instead became filled with anger against him. They seized him tyrannically and forcibly, deposed him, and ordained him anew.
He beat his face, and his eyes grew dim, and he became blind.
And while he was now weeping and lamenting over himself, and striving to run to the house of refuge of repentance, the end of his departure overtook him;
And his old age went down to Sheol in torment and grief, while his judgment is kept for the righteous Judge.
John’s advisers took a document and wrote it as though it came from Paul himself, putting these words into it: “I, Paul, who was astray and lost,
when I came to understand the true faith, turned back and came willingly and of my own free choice,
not under compulsion or constraint, to the church of God, to you, my lord John, the ecumenical patriarch.
I acknowledge in this document that I assent to the council of the six hundred and thirty holy fathers who assembled in the city of Chalcedon,
and to the letter of the holy and blessed pope of Rome, in accordance with the confession of Peter, chief of the apostles, until my last breath.
And there shall never again be any reversal or change from it on my part. These things I have confessed and sealed with my own hand.
I, Paul the bishop, acknowledge that I agree with and accept everything written in this document.
They therefore brought this to him for his signature, but did not allow him to read and learn what they had written in his name and as though it came from him, falsely and deceitfully.
And they bore false witness against him, without fear of God.
This Deuterius, diligent and upright in his conduct, who from his youth until his old age, throughout a period of thirty-five years,
labored with John, who was making disciples of the pagans in the regions of Asia, Caria, Phrygia, and Lydia,
and together with him established ninety-nine new churches and twelve monasteries—John relied on him and trusted him more than the others.

John also appointed him bishop of the orthodox in the region of Caria and made him his successor, since he himself had grown old and advanced in years and had become caught up in the struggle of persecution.
He appointed him over all the churches and monasteries, and he labored, visited them, and supported them all until the end of his life,
which came in the imperial city. This Deuterius, aided by divine grace, ran the race of his ministry with strength,
and boldly and valiantly; and while the Synodites were running after him to seize him and do to him as they had done to Paul:
and install him in that man's place in Antioch, the Lord did not deliver him into their hands. Thus he completed his struggle and departed in a good old age.
As for this group, these are the people who oppose the treatise that Theodosius of Alexandria composed
while he was in the royal city, opposing two heresies, namely that of the Tritheists and that of the Sabellians.
They take offense at certain statements in it and suppose that he too introduces a plurality of substances and natures.
For this reason they separate themselves and assemble on their own, although they have no leader and no one to ordain priests for them.
These people often sought to unite with the faithful, and discussions were held with them. Some of them did unite,
those among whom there was knowledge, so that they might judge properly; and others of them, again, without knowledge, foolishly, and without proper cause, thus craftily persisted.
Now these Cappadocian monks, at the height of the persecution, as I also mentioned them in the earlier account,
They were persecuted and left the great and strong monastery in Cappadocia called that of Gordision [?]:
They numbered no fewer than seventy men, venerable and zealous elders. After building and establishing many places,
and being driven again from place to place, they went and found a good, secure place, suitable in every way for their monastery,
called Cardonian, near the hot springs called Pythia, on the southern side of the imperial city.
A certain chamberlain, one of the faithful, bought it for them, and they settled there. They planted a vineyard there and built a large church.
That entire company of venerable elders died, and the younger generation remained.
and at last, when King Justin and the queen and the whole senate were passing by on their way to the hot springs, they entered and lodged in the monastery;
And through promises and gifts they brought them into submission, while he ordered that their former monastery, from which they had been driven out, should also be restored

to them, and that they should be granted exemption from taxes. In this way they brought them into submission and stamped them with their seal, after twenty years in which they had struggled through the trials of persecution.
They divided: half of them returned and took possession of their former monastery, while half remained in that same place.
They were thrown into confusion and dismay, so to speak, so that their ship was wrecked at the entrance to the harbor. And they turned away completely from all orthodoxy.

As for these monasteries, then, both the large ones and the small ones for women, some of them were subjected to pressure and submitted, while others held out—or, even if they eventually turned back, remained in this condition:
those who had submitted and those who had not submitted joined together in their entire service, except for receiving communion together.
Even at the Eucharist that the clergy celebrated in each of them,
during the waving they stood together and took part in the service, performing the whole order of worship, and they could not separate.
But those who did not receive communion also had other, orthodox priests who celebrated the Eucharist and gave it to them.
Because of the distress of the times, they could not act otherwise, lest they immediately be expelled and scattered.
And the leaders of the orthodox were compelled to remain silent and overlook these things, so that orthodoxy would not disappear altogether.
It happens, however, to people whose [?] lot it is to suffer mockery and to be made a laughing-stock;
that in these narratives we make use of an account concerning unsightly animals, namely elephants.
We bring this to remembrance not casually or, so to speak, contemptuously, but first of all for the glory of God,
and secondly as a rebuke and a disgrace to pagans, Jews, and the rest of those who are astray,
who deny the cross and reject the work of our salvation, which was accomplished through the sign of the cross.
For these elephants, through the victory that God gave the Christians over the accursed people of the Magi,
were taken from them and brought up to the imperial city. They remained there for a long time.
Whenever they passed in front of churches, the first one, which went at the head, would turn toward the east, lower its head and trunk, and bow down.
Immediately it would raise its trunk, move it around, and make the shape of a cross. It would make the sign and then pass on.
The one behind it followed and acted in the same way, and so did the rest, one after another, however many there were.
We saw this many times with our own eyes, marveling and giving thanks to God, who had given knowledge of Christianity
even to dumb animals, as a rebuke to rational beings who neglect Christianity and reject the grace of the Savior of our race.
Another thing of the same kind, also worthy of wonder and great amazement, was continually done by these animals.
Whenever there was a hippikos—that is, the customary horse race—
Steadily those elephants kept coming in, with a man riding on each one of them who guided them.
They would stand in the middle of the Hippodrome, facing the emperor. As far as they could, and as their nature allowed them to bend down,
they would bow down and pay homage to him. Each one would make the sign of the cross with its lip and trace it facing the emperor.
The crowds gathered there were astonished and amazed at how they made the sign of the cross as perfectly as human beings.
Then, after receiving gifts from the emperor, they would leave.
Now, at the end of Tiberius’s reign and the beginning of Maurice’s, a disaster—that is, a great fire—occurred throughout the center of the imperial city.
There was complete destruction: many properties, large, medium, and small alike, were laid waste.
Even those who escaped were stripped and deprived of all their possessions and all their wealth, which, as they watched, became food for the flames in a single day.
Since, therefore, it happens that people advanced in knowledge come upon readers of these histories:
may pour blame on the writer because the account of a single event sometimes appears in several chapters, mixed together and scattered about,
let those who find fault with these things know this: most of these accounts were written during a time of persecution and distress, amid every kind of opposition.
Under the pressure of necessity, the sheets on which these chapters were being written were carried away to various places, along with the remaining papers and other books.
Sometimes they remained hidden in different places for as long as two or three years.
It happened that matters arose which the writer wished to put on record, and some of them had already been recorded in earlier chapters.
But the earlier notebooks were not at hand for him to read and determine whether these matters had been written down.
Nor did he remember that they had already been written down, so he subsequently recorded them again. For this reason,
In some places it is found that a record about one and the same subject has been made in several chapters.
Time did not even allow a later comparison of them to be made readily and easily.
Since, then, Eutychius the patriarch — how greatly the vainglory of his heart led him astray! — had from the beginning belonged to the heresy of the [?]:
When he became bishop, he wanted to conceal his heresy and please those who had appointed him,
who held the Chalcedonian position. At first he stood up and vigorously championed the doctrine of two natures, beginning to persecute harshly.
When he was removed from his see and went into exile, he undertook to compose a large book of divisive teaching about two natures.
When he was recalled and returned to his see after John’s death, as we also explained in the preceding account,
he began sending this book to the great senatorial households, to men and women, especially those who recoiled from the confession of two natures.
He wrote to them: “Read and learn that the Church confesses two natures in Christ after the union.”
While they were laughing at his foolishness, they sent him his book. Then again, after a short delay, he heard about the heresy of Athanasius:
He was the one who, in the heresy of those who count substances—that is, beings and natures—in the Holy Trinity,
he had become its head and establisher, since he too had been led astray by the error of John Grammaticus of Alexandria:
He said that these human bodies do not rise at the resurrection of the dead, but that other bodies come into being and rise instead.
As a result of this madness of paganism and Manichaeism, a division arose among them, and they anathematized one another in writing.
When Patriarch Eutychius learned of these things, he immediately joined them, became entangled with them, and became one of them. He began composing teaching on this subject.
He wrote and published books, until even his own bishops and clergy were stirred up and rose against him, and much was said between them.
Thus he was refuted and fell silent, and he suppressed his book, although he did not abandon that belief.
As he also tells us in another chapter, that excellent Eutychius was zealously and fiercely opposed to the words, “You were crucified for us.”
He wrote everywhere and issued threats, pressing the bishops to remove this confession from their churches and cities.
From the other bishops whom he newly appointed, he demanded pledges that they would abolish this confession in their territories.
As they took care to do as they had been commanded, scandal and blasphemy arose in the cities and rural districts—that is, in the villages and throughout the regions—
especially those of Syria, Asia, and Cappadocia, which had held to this confession from the beginning. Consequently, in many villages
and cities they disputed and rose up, saying, “Even if we are cut to pieces and burned, we will not deny God, who was crucified and suffered for us.”
This dispute and struggle persisted everywhere, even after the death of Eutychius.
The second book of the Ecclesiastical History ends here. It contains fifty-two chapters.
