As for the origin of the cause—the submission of the Armenians under Persian rule to the Romans—
The rest of the church histories from before these events have been told to us in brief records. So now let us turn our account to the events that follow.
For the Persian king was carried away by pride because he had captured Dara, and the arrogance of his heart led him astray.
So, trusting that there was no war in the regions of Syria, he gathered his army and set out confidently for Armenia.
He had set his sights on Theodosiopolis, on the border of his own Armenia, and on Caesarea in Cappadocia and the other cities.
He was so confident that, when Theodore the silentiary had been sent to him on an embassy, and he decided to go out to war, he took Theodore with him. When Theodore begged him to release him,
As he was travelling, he said to him: "Come with me to Armenia. You will enter Theodosiopolis with me, and you will bathe and rest there."
Then I will release you.” So he took him along and brought him with him to Armenia, firmly confident that he would enter and capture the city without difficulty.
When the Roman armies learned of these things, although they trembled greatly at the king's name, they made thorough preparations to face him.
When he saw these powerful armies, he was greatly dismayed, for they were said to number more than one hundred and twenty thousand.
When they challenged him and prepared to fight him, he became afraid and turned away from them to advance against another city.
But there too they hurried to confront him, met him, and drove him away from that place as well.
And once they had tested his strength, they grew still bolder against him and despised him. After this, when he saw that things had not turned out as he wished,
he set out into the northern mountains and turned toward Cappadocia, intending to enter and conquer Caesarea.
When the Roman armies saw this, they moved against him and reached Cappadocia ahead of him.
They stood against him and hemmed him in there in the mountains of Cappadocia. They held him back and did not let him pass.
They skirmished with one another for many days, while he did not dare engage them in a pitched battle.
When he saw that they were more numerous and stronger than he was, and that he could not get past them and march on Caesarea,
he became bewildered and deeply troubled. From then on he planned how he might get through and escape to his own country. His Magi, however, reproached him and argued with him.
Then he turned and went out into Cappadocia toward Sebaste, while they were all trembling before the Roman armies.
Out of shame, so that he would not be reproached for having been unable to accomplish any of his plans, he attacked Sebaste and burned it with fire.
For he found neither plunder nor captives, because the whole region had been evacuated before his arrival.
When he passed on from there, he made a retreat and now headed eastward, to escape to his own country if he could.
Then the Roman forces held him in contempt: they spied out his army, despised it, and took courage against him.
When he saw that they had surrounded him and were pressing upon him from every side, he was forced to flee hastily to the mountain,
abandoning his entire camp and his pavilion—that is, his tent—and all his equipment and his treasures of gold, silver, and pearls,
and all his splendid royal garments, and to flee empty-handed. Then the Romans hurried in and took possession of his entire camp.
They killed everyone they overtook there and carried off all his equipment and that of his nobles,
as well as the shrine of the fire he worshiped and the horses that carried it and bore it in procession.
People became rich from what they took there. Indeed, some of the Romans who found and took the royal possessions formed a band, took what they had found, and fled.
They were never found or seen again. But those who fled and escaped from the Persian camp
went to the king, weeping and saying, “My lord, the Romans fell upon us and killed many of your servants.
They plundered and carried off our entire camp.” When he heard this, he reportedly answered them, “Leave them alone.”
For he ordered his entire army to surround him and raise a wall of shields for him. He arranged them in ranks.
He rode among them on horseback and pleaded with them, showing them his white hair and saying,
“My brothers and my sons, have pity on my white hair! Go in and fight for the Persian kingdom, so that it will not be mocked and laughed at.
Look, I myself am fighting alongside you like any one of you horsemen.” For his nobles, it is said, were constantly arguing with him, saying:
“Whether we live or die,” they said, “Persia gains a bad name through us, for none of the Persian kings has ever done what you have done,
bringing us here to die in these mountains.” The Romans learned from some of them what was being said among them.
The Persians scattered again, and they threw themselves to another side to escape to the city.
They came out opposite Melitene. If there had not been jealousy and divisions among the Roman commanders,
and they had agreed with one another, they would have finished him and his entire army there. They had given one another their word, divided their forces, and surrounded him.
They turned toward Justinian the patrician, the son of Germanus, and Justinian became afraid and fled before him. His fellow commanders did not reach him and help him either.
When he saw this, he and his army took heart, grew bold, entered Melitene, and set it on fire.
When the Persian entered the city of Melitene, he immediately gave the order, and the whole city was burned.
When he went out to cross the Euphrates, heading toward his own country, the commanders of the Roman armies sent him this message:
“What you have done—entering and burning the city—is not the proper conduct of a king: to carry out raids and roam about.
For us, who are servants of the king, these things you have done would have been deeply disgraceful if we had committed them,
All the more so for you, since you think of yourself not only as a king but as king of kings.
For it is not fitting for a king to behave like those who go out on raids, plundering and fleeing, setting fires and burning things.
Rather, a king should take his stand openly in battle, with authority, confidence, and royal dignity.
When he wins, he should triumph as a king, not enter like a thief, cause destruction, steal, and flee.
Instead, get ready, and now let us face one another in open battle, so that it may be clearly known to whom victory and defeat belong.”
When he heard this, he ordered a battle for the next day on the plain east of the city, some distance from it.
Early in the morning, both sides drew up their ranks opposite one another, with only a short distance between them.
They stood in formation, looking at one another, from morning until the sixth hour, and not a man moved from his place.
The king himself stood behind his army, and they watched one another to see who would begin first.
The men who recounted all these things to us, who had been interpreters for the Persians and the Romans, swore to us,
“Finally, three of us spurred our horses and rode out from the Roman ranks into the space between the two sides.
We galloped as far as the front of the Persian ranks and then galloped back again, without approaching them. We did this three times,
making our horses gallop, while both sides turned and watched us. For we had ridden out to provoke them to battle.
Yet not one of them moved from his place and came out to meet us. They stood in formation like a wall.”
They did not even send word to one another. But finally, it is said, he sent word: “There will be no battle today now, for the time has passed.”
And so the armies withdrew from one another. During the night, before dawn broke, the king and his army were found beside the Euphrates River,
as he sought a way and made every effort to cross the river, which is six miles from Melitene.
For the Romans were pursuing him, intending to trap him against the river and destroy him. This they indeed did, and the Persians were thrown into confusion.
When the Persian army saw the Roman army advancing behind them, they plunged into the river on their horses.
More than half his army sank and drowned. He and the rest escaped with difficulty and crossed over, some on horses and some by swimming.
They hurried through Roman Armenia. As they marched in haste, he ordered them to burn every village they encountered.
Thus he turned aside into the high, barren mountains, where there had never been a road. He was compelled to send his army ahead of him to make a road for him.
They cut through thickets of trees, and in some places they dug into the mountains themselves and cut through them to make a road for him.
Thus, bewildered and troubled in spirit, he barely escaped from the hands of the Romans and entered his own country with great difficulty.
And so, it is said, he issued a decree and established a law that a king should never again go out to battle unless he was going out against another king.
As for the commanders of the Romans, after they had distinguished themselves with great victories and prevailed in many battles,
and had destroyed most of those against whom they were sent, and had conquered and subdued all those northern peoples who had been subject to the Persians,
and had advanced and laid waste to Persian territory for many stages of the journey, coming within three stages of the Persian royal capital,
and had plundered and carried off the Persians’ elephants and filled Constantinople with elephants, and had distinguished themselves in many deeds beyond telling,
and all Persia had trembled before them—finally, when the king of the Persians returned to his own country in the year eight hundred and eighty of Alexander,
the Romans thereafter became carefree and puffed up with pride, like men who had boldly confronted a king and stood against him.
From then on they went about without fear, thinking that they were now free and at rest from all wars and fighting.
All the troops were encamped confidently and at ease, having taken off their armor and turned all their horses loose at pasture.
Then suddenly their scouting party—that is, their scouts—arrived and said:
“Get up! Arm yourselves! The Persian army is coming against you with Tamkhosrau the marzban.
Look to your own safety!” When they heard this, they mocked and scorned them, saying:
“Could these men dare to show themselves before us?” And they did not trouble themselves or take care to prepare.
While they were still speaking, the Persian army suddenly appeared before them, not prepared to fight them, but merely to show themselves.
When they saw them advancing in great ranks stretched out like walls, trembling and fear fell upon them all at once, and they were thrown into confusion.
They had not even gathered their horses together. They were occupied with eating, drinking, and luxury, and they were drunk.
Everyone who saw this was alarmed, and they began to flee headlong. Others, seeing the others fleeing, panicked and fled as well.
When the army commanders saw that they had been left deserted and that the army had fled from them, they too fled.
Everyone who could take his weapons and seize his horse mounted and fled.
Some fled on foot carrying their weapons. When they grew tired from running, they threw their weapons onto the road and fled unarmed.
Some who were riding horses with their weapons threw their weapons away when they grew tired. If their horses then grew weak, they dismounted and fled on foot.
Thus the Persians went after them without hurrying, not even pursuing them,
but laughing, mocking, and jeering at them. For they numbered a hundred and twenty thousand, while these Persians numbered no more than thirty thousand.
Thus they were terrified and fled from them, though they had neither trembled before their king nor fled from him.
Thus, in the end, all the Roman armies, together with their commanders, brought shame and a bad name upon themselves.
The Persians had not even drawn a sword against them, nor had they drawn a bow and shot a single arrow at them. Yet they gathered up all their weapons and [?],
and coats of mail, shields, helmets, javelins, swords, lances, bows, and quivers filled with countless arrows.
For afterward everyone was saying and repeating that this was because the Romans had angered God
when they entered these northern regions, whose inhabitants were Christians. The priests would take the Gospel book and crosses and come out to meet them,
but they paid them no attention. In the end, these Romans, behaving wantonly without fear of God,
would take little children one and two years old. Some would seize each child by a foot and toss him as high as they could,
and others would catch them on lances and swords as they came down, impale them, and throw them to the dogs.
They also abused, killed, and plundered monks. They also brought out recluses, aged and venerable men, from the cells where they had been confined for many years,
and hung them up and tortured them, cutting their thighs with swords while saying to them, “Bring gold and silver.”
They also reportedly tortured women who were nuns in this same way, until they suffered a bitter death.
Through these evil deeds, which they were reportedly committing, they angered God. He put them to shame and broke them before their enemies, and they could not stand against them.
Now, concerning the reason why the Armenians under Persian rule came and surrendered to the Romans, and concerning that time, the many battles, and the devastation that occurred there,
and concerning those who went up to the imperial capital and were received by the emperor and honored with high offices and many gifts,
Stories like these are covered in the earlier chapters, in the brief records about them.
But what we now wish to make known in our account is that, when our Roman emperor faced all these conflicts with the Persians:
that he should not hand over those who had come and sought refuge with him because of their Christianity. Afterward, the emperor enriched virtually all the Armenians with presents and great gifts.
He also granted them exemption from taxation for three years. The Persian king kept sending him the message, “Give me my subjects who have rebelled against me,” but he would not comply.
The Persian king, however, made arrangements and gave the Armenians a written promise that he would do them no harm and would not hold their offense against them.
Then they turned away from the Romans and went and handed over the whole country to him, apart from those leaders who were with the emperor in Constantinople.
That is, the whole population of the country, about twenty thousand, went back and submitted to the Persians. He once again took possession of Armenia, as before.
Their leaders were a man named Vardan and the others with him, together with the king of the people called Gurgenes.
with all his people who had submitted to the Romans, he too remained in the imperial capital in great honor, because they had come and submitted to Emperor Justin,
in the fifth year of his reign, which was the year eight hundred and eighty-two of Alexander. The war on their account, in turn, continued for years.
Again, in the year eight hundred and eighty-seven, three senators were sent on an embassy to the border region:
Theodore the patrician, son of Peter the master of offices, and John and Peter, consuls from the family of Emperor Anastasius, together with Zachariah the Syrian, a physician and sophist.
Then Mebodes and the rest came from the Persian side too, and they camped next to Dara, which the Persians were holding.
to discuss and examine together what had taken place in the two states.
Each side turned against the other, saying, “You violated your obligations in this affair and that.”
The other side, in turn, brought further accusations, saying, “You broke the peace between the two states
and crossed over and devastated our territories.” The others said, “Your Arabs crossed over and committed outrages in our territory.”
In this way they sat facing one another, raising accusations, disputes, and inquiries of this kind against each other, until they came to quarrels and insults.
They spent more than a year speaking and listening in this way, while each side kept its own ruler informed.
The God-loving Caesar Tiberius was sending and receiving replies, because Emperor Justin was ill.
Although both sides wanted peace between them, each displayed a tough stance toward the other, so as not to lower itself before the other and appear weak.
For the Caesar of the Romans had sent word to the Persians: "We take far more pleasure in good peace than in war.
If you want peace, we do not refuse it. But if you want battle, we are no weaker than you. We are ready to meet you."
The Persian king, however, had in mind that, because he had been given three hundredweights to make peace for three years,
he would likewise receive a hundredweight for every year if he made peace with the Romans.
When Caesar learned of this, he wrote and sent him this message: “You are gravely mistaken if you think
that the Roman Empire will give you a single mina in exchange for peace, or if you imagine that we buy peace with gold.
But if you wish there to be peace between us, with both kingdoms showing equal honor to each other, let it be so. Otherwise, prepare for war.
When the Persian received such a decision, he was considerably shaken by the message.
Nevertheless, he agreed to an equal peace without gold. Then, when Caesar received this reply, he wrote back:
“You should know that the kingdom of the Romans has never been lowly. Rather, it is powerful and has never been subject to anyone.
And I do not know how the former emperors stooped to giving the Persians five hundred pounds of gold every year.
But you should know that the kingdom of the Romans will never again give even five minas, either to you or to anyone else.
For your envoys were boasting among the barbarian people of the Turks, saying, ‘The Romans are slaves,
and like contemptible slaves they pay us tribute.’ Unless you put an end to this, we will have no peace with you.”
And when much had been settled [?]—that is, immediately—he not only gave a plain order but at once stopped the tribute as well.
He prepared copies of the peace documents and sent them to the envoys at the frontier.
Then, when Caesar saw that he had yielded to these demands, he sent him this message: “Give us the city of Dara now, and we will make peace.”
When the Persian received this, he was greatly disturbed by it. He wrote: “I took Dara according to the laws of war.
But you have taken and occupied the territories of our Armenian subjects without war. Give me Armenia, and I will give you Dara.”
Caesar, however, was reluctant to hand over the Armenians, because they were Christians and had submitted to the Christian kingdom for that very reason.
For this reason, the envoys of the two sides fell into a great dispute with one another, until they threatened to meet each other with the sword.
And so they parted from one another, embittered against each other, and the prospect of peace was completely broken off.
Both kingdoms were now preparing for battle.
The Persian envoy summoned his commanders and instructed them, saying: “Go and keep watch over the frontiers, for the Romans will not make peace.”
So Adarmahan, the great marzban of the Persians, who had discussed peace with the Roman envoys, as soon as they decided that there would be no more peace,
in his anger and bitterness at having been insulted by the envoys, gathered an army and marched out. He devastated and completely burned the whole districts of Dara, Tella, and Tell-Beshme,
and the district of Reshaina—its fortified villages, churches, monasteries, and the whole countryside. He devastated, burned, and killed, and came against Tella and said to its people:
“Surrender the city to us, so that what happened to the people of Dara does not happen to you too, and you perish.
Where are those envoys of yours who were threatening us? Let them come out now and face us!”
But the people of Tella said to them: “We cannot surrender to you now,
because we have received letters saying that the patrician Justinian has set out to come here, and that he has sixty thousand Lombards with him.”
And if we surrender to you now, he will come and immediately wipe us off the face of the earth.
And so they withdrew from them, after burning the great and imposing church of the Mother of God outside the city.

Along with the rest of their other evil deeds, they returned to Dara, mocking the Romans and boasting of the devastation they had inflicted, the captives they had taken, and the great amount of plunder they had carried away.
Now the commanders of the Roman army were not getting along with one another, and they were writing to the emperor about one another and against one another.
So when that God-loving emperor looked to one of his own men named Maurice, whom he had appointed to the position of count of the Excubitors,
and who was therefore called count, he summoned him and ordered him to go down to the East as chief of all the military commanders.
He gave him authority to provide for, organize and command all the stratelates and tribunes of the whole army,
None of them was to dare to disobey his command or the word of his mouth in any way.
He gave him authority to enlist men and discharge from service whomever he wished, and sent him with many hundredweights of money to provision the troops.
Even before this, he had sent a praetorian prefect named Gregory to administer and attend to the expenses of the troops.
He had achieved success in everything there in Armenia. As for the illustrious Maurice, when he received his orders and was sent out, he first went to his homeland, Cappadocia.
For he too was a Cappadocian. He immediately gathered and enlisted many Romans. He also took with him many Excubitors and scribones, and whatever troops were available.
He also gathered and enlisted many people from among the Urtaye and the Syrians. He went and encamped between Armenia and Syria,
namely, at Citharizon. He sent for all the military commanders, assembled them, and spoke with them. He organized them, gave them orders, and strengthened and encouraged them.
He stayed there for two months, and his reputation spread. Fear of him fell upon all the Persians, who saw that the Roman troops were more numerous and stronger than they were.
While they were there, fear fell upon them. They devised a trick and set off toward Persian Armenia.
They sent word to those stationed in Theodosiopolis: “After thirty days, be ready and face us in battle.”
When the Romans received this message, they sent word to Count Maurice, who in turn ordered the entire army to prepare for battle.
But as soon as the Persians had sent this communication, they made cunning preparations to deceive the Romans.
They prepared, gathered their army, and passed through their own territory. They then emerged secretly into Roman territory from the direction of Martyropolis.
They began devastating and burning the whole region of Sophanene, especially all the churches and monasteries,
and the whole region of Amida and the whole country. They came against Amida and burned everything around it, right up to its wall.
all the churches and great monasteries around it. They remained outside the city for three days.
When they saw that they could not overcome its defenses, and also feared that Maurice might catch up with them with his army and wreak destruction upon them,
they burned and plundered the whole region of Mesopotamia in one sweep. Then they turned back and entered their own country.
How, while the Romans were preparing for battle, the Persians deceived them.
Finally, like thieves and a raiding band, they came out and burned and devastated all Mesopotamia and carried its people into captivity, in the year eight hundred and eighty-eight of Alexander.
In that same year Maurice had also come down from the imperial capital, and so, in a hurried rush,
they took captives and everything they found and fled to their own country out of fear of the Romans. In about eighteen days they inflicted all this destruction and returned.
For when Count Maurice heard these things, he was deeply disturbed and embittered. He gathered his entire army
and headed straight for Arzon, a fertile region belonging to the Persians, in a surge of anger, because the Persians had mocked and ridiculed him.

They entered, devastated and uprooted, and took a great many of the inhabitants captive. They conquered and advanced as far as the Tigris. He went down, took captives, uprooted, and burned the entire region.
Because they were sincere Christians, without deceit, they would come out to meet the armies and their commanders in a religious procession, with crosses and the Gospel.
They asked them for a pledge that their lives would be spared, saying, “Have mercy on us, for we are Christians like you.
"For we too are ready to serve the Christian king."
When Maurice and the others heard these things from many of them, they showed mercy,
saying to them, “Any of you who wants to live and serve the Christian emperor should take his possessions and load everything he has onto his pack animal,
and he will live, and we will not kill him. But if we find him here after two or three days, he will die.”
And so most of them—all who escaped the sword—fled and went into Roman territory: the greater part of the population of Arzanene.
When these things became known to the emperor, he gave orders, and they were sent to the island of Cyprus.
They were distributed among the villages throughout the island and remained there. But those Persians who had slipped away and crossed into Roman territory
and set fires, trembling before Maurice lest he overtake them in his onslaught, hurried and burned as much as they could in fifteen days.
And so, trembling, they fled and crossed back into their own country before Maurice could overtake them.
Again Maurice and al-Mundhir, son of al-Harith, king of the Arabs, gathered their armies together and crossed into Persian territory by the desert route.
They entered and advanced many stages into Persian territory, as far as Beth Aramaye. When they reached the great bridge in Beth Aramaye,
which they were counting on crossing to conquer the great cities of the Persian kingdom, they found the bridge destroyed.
The Persians had destroyed it when they learned of their approach. Thus they and their armies experienced great hardship, especially the Romans.
They began quarreling with one another and turned back, having been unable to accomplish anything useful.
Only with difficulty and hardship did they manage to escape and return to Roman territory, writing bitter accusations against one another.
Maurice suspected al-Mundhir of having sent word ahead to inform the Persians, so that they destroyed the bridge to prevent them from crossing.
This was deceit. The king had a great deal of trouble, sending to the chiefs and working to reconcile them firmly with one another,
Finally Maurice himself went up to the king, and it was not known whether he accused Mundhir.
When the Persians saw that Maurice and Mundhir had gone down to their own country, and saw that the country had been emptied of troops,
the Persian governor, whose name was Adarmahan, crossed into Roman territory with a large army.
He came to the territories of Tella and Reshaina, and destroyed and burned what they had previously left untouched.
They crossed into the fertile territory of Edessa, and burned, destroyed, and devastated the whole country of Osrhoene.
while he went about the country confidently and without fear.
as though he were in his own country, he stayed for many days, leaving no house standing wherever he passed.
He mocked the entire Roman army, which had been unable to oppose him. Finally, when Maurice and Mundhir had come up from Persian territory and were moving down,
and he heard that they intended to march against him, he sent them this mocking message: “Since I have heard that you are preparing to come against me,
do not tire yourselves by coming, for you are worn out by the hardships of the journey. Instead, rest, and I will come to you.”

Finally, after the devastation, plundering, and taking of captives that he had carried out, and after he had taken captives and done everything he wanted, he heard that they intended to march against him.
He took away all the booty and all the captives he had taken, withdrew from the territory of the Edessenes and went back to his own country,
and nobody stopped him, out of two hundred thousand Romans who were eating the king's rations.
But when he set off to leave, they went out to march against him. When they failed to catch up with him, they said, “He has fled!”
Now the entire army of the Persian Arabs gathered against Mundhir son of Harith, and the Persian army itself also prepared to join them,
to go up and attack Mundhir after he had come up from Persian territory. When he learned of this, like a warrior, he did not delay.
Instead, he immediately gathered his army and advanced against them by a desert route, sending scouts and learning where they were and how many they were.
Suddenly he attacked them while they were unaware, startling them, throwing them into confusion, devastating them, and destroying them.
He seized some of them, bound them, and put them in fetters. Only a few of them escaped. From there he headed straight for their city of Hira,
and devastated and burned it. He went on and returned with great plunder and many captives, having won a magnificent victory.
After Dara, Apamea, and the other places had been taken captive, and the Persians had brought all their captives into Persian territory,
when these were counted at Nisibis before the king, their number came to two hundred and seventy-five thousand.
Those remaining who had not been distributed he brought in and confined in Antioch, the city he had built for himself when he conquered Antioch and carried off its inhabitants.
He built a city in his own country bearing its name, and there he also confined all the captives he had taken from Antioch and its entire surrounding district.
In it he also imprisoned the people of Dara and Apamea, together with all the other captives whom he took afterward.
Even in their imprisonment and under the strict guard in which they were kept, these people did not stop devising schemes.
They had supposedly been maintained there to give help, but they had made a secret pact with one of the Persians, namely those who were guarding them and guarding the wall.
They collected money and gave him five hundred coins to lower two of them by a rope at night from the place where he kept watch.
There were also some blessed men there, Arab monks, one of whom was named Benjamin,
and the other, who was his disciple, Samuel. They made preparations so that, if they got out and escaped from there,
he would immediately make his way to the emperor of the Romans and inform him about the many thousands of captives imprisoned there in Antioch.
All the captives also sent word through him: “There are more than thirty thousand of us imprisoned here,
and the Persians guarding us number no more than five hundred men. If one of the Roman commanders is sent
and merely appears outside the city, we will kill the Persians, get out, and escape into Roman territory.”
So, when all the captives had secretly said these things to that blessed man,
the Persian who had taken the bribe lowered him and those with him from the wall by ropes at night, and they fled and escaped into Roman territory.
He first informed the Roman commanders of these things. They in turn wrote and sent him to the emperor.
When he reached the imperial capital, he came to us.
He informed the master of offices of these things, and the latter went in and informed Emperor Tiberius. But the emperor disregarded them and apparently did not consider them true.
Thus the matter of rescuing that whole oppressed body of captives was neglected and abandoned.
It is therefore not inappropriate, even though we are writing about a Magian and an enemy, to give an account also of the reign and death of Khosrow, king of the Persians.
As his own deeds testify, he was shrewd and wise, and throughout his life he devoted himself to reading philosophy.
It is said that he took care to collect all the books of all the religions, reading and examining them all,
to discover which were truthful and wise, and which were worthless and full of falsehood and empty tales.
As he read and examined them all, it is said, he praised the books of the Christians above all the others, saying, “These are more truthful and wiser than those of all the religions.”
For this reason, it is said, he devoted himself especially to them, reading them and believing their teachings. For this reason, too, he did not appear to hate the Christians.
Even though the Magi stirred him up against the Christians, he was not often seen to order persecution against the Christians.
For at one time the catholicos of the Nestorians, who was constantly with him, had brought accusations against those few orthodox bishops
who were in Persia, since all the bishops throughout Persia were Nestorians.
And few among them were orthodox. So, when the catholicos was making harsh accusations against these people,
the king ordered them to come and debate one another before him about their faith,
so that he too might learn and examine for himself what was being said by them and among them, judge their statements, and find out which of them spoke reasonably.
So, when these orthodox believers arrived, he ordered everyone belonging to the two sides to assemble and come before him.
When they came before him, and the two sides stood before him on either side—the leader of the orthodox being a bishop,
a holy man named Ahudemmeh—the king ordered them to debate and tell one another what they had to say about their faith.
When the catholicos and those with him began speaking with the orthodox, they listened patiently to him, and he began and finished.
Then they spoke, refuted all his statements, and confounded him, taking the king himself as judge.
Since the things said in debate between them were numerous and are not easy to write down, we have left them aside.
Then King Khosrow himself accepted and praised what the orthodox had said. He said to the catholicos,
“These men know what they are talking about and can establish and substantiate their statements, which seem to me, too, to be very sound.
But yours are confused and muddled and have no foundation. You do not even appear able to establish your own statements.
Nor do they seem to me to have the solidity and truth of what these men have said.
From this I have learned that you accused them before me unjustly and improperly.
Now that I have seen and heard for myself, I order you not to encroach upon them or harass them again.”
When he gave these orders, all the orthodox fell down and bowed before him. They acknowledged his kindness, saying,
“My lord, they persecute us, attack us, and plunder us. They destroy our churches and monasteries
and do not allow us to offer prayers and supplications to God in them for the continuance and preservation of your life and your kingdom.”
Then he gave them a firm order: “Go and build your churches and monasteries, and no one shall again have authority to harass you.”
And so, after bowing before him and praying for him, they returned to their own regions with great joy.
From then on, all the orthodox in the Persian territories went about with great freedom and without fear.
When they received this order, they took courage and undertook a great enterprise:
they too would appoint a catholicos through the blessed Mar Jacob, bishop of the orthodox, from that time onward.
This had never before happened or been done in the land of the Persians. From then until today, a catholicos of the faithful has remained firmly established.
So let no one suppose that we have brought his story to remembrance because we wish to praise a Magian.
But concerning this, as it is said in Samson’s riddle, “Out of the eater came food, and out of the bitter came sweetness.”
He was indeed so very bitter! What more, then, is there to say about a pagan and misguided man?
But for the sake of those things that serve the purpose of these histories, we come to an outline of his story.
So when the peace between the frontiers was broken, he made out that he was in distress and poverty, so that, as people were saying,
the documents of the peace between them went before him, tied up and suspended toward heaven, when he came against Dara.
He said, “See, great God, for you know that I did not desire, nor do I desire, all this devastation
and the shedding of human blood that has taken place in both states.” Again, even when his death was near, he showed that he had humbled himself and wanted peace.
he thought that for every year he kept the peace he would receive a centenarium of gold, following the custom of the three years that had gone by.
When the Roman and Persian envoys met at the frontier for negotiations and to discuss peace, as we explained above,
then the victorious Tiberius, who was still Caesar during Justin’s lifetime, and whom all the Persians feared,
showed himself courageous and took his stand, saying, “The Roman Empire is neither inferior nor subject to the Persian Empire.
We will not give a single hundred-pound payment in exchange for peace.
Unless there is peace with equal honor for the empires, I will never make peace with them at all.”
This disturbed the Persian king considerably. He even gathered his Magi and said to them,
“We have now learned that the Caesar who has arisen among the Romans is a young man, youthful and warlike.
As for me, you see that I have grown old, and I can no longer endure the hardships of war. So let us now make peace with the Romans, because we cannot withstand their strength.”
Thus they took counsel and sent this message: “So that you may not think that I am eager for gold and value gold more highly than peace,
let us now make peace with equal honor for the empires, and let the devastation cease. I ask for nothing.”
When he had promised this, the victorious Caesar Tiberius hurled another missile at him, saying,
“Do not even suppose that you will receive another single mina of the gold that you have been receiving from the Romans until now.
For the Roman Empire has not sunk so low as to pay tribute to the Persians.”
In reply to this, the Persian sent word: “That payment of gold was established by earlier emperors; it was not you who established it.
But know that peace is far dearer to me than anything else. I will give up these hundred-pound payments too, and let us make peace.”
When Caesar saw that the Persian had humbled himself and come to these terms, he sent him this message: “Unless you give us Dara, we will not make peace with you.”
At this the Persians were thrown into turmoil, and the peace was broken. They withdrew from the frontier in hostility, to wage war against one another.
Immediately the sword was unleashed in both realms. And immediately, at that same time, King Khosrow died, in the year eight hundred and ninety.
His son became king. According to their reckoning, Khosrow himself had reigned for forty-eight years.
When King Khosrow died, one of his sons, named Hormizd, became king after him.
As his accomplishments are recounted, his own deeds also show
"He is an arrogant, boorish and light-minded boy." So when he became king, like a madman lacking sense,
he became so conceited and puffed up that he would not even send the customary token of his accession to the Roman emperor, as kings normally did.
Caesar Tiberius did not stop paying the customary symbolon [payment] of the kingdom, even though the kingdoms were deeply at odds and at war.
Rather, as soon as he took his seat as Caesar, he sent Khosrow gifts as a token of his accession, just as Khosrow, when he became king, had sent them to Emperor Justinian,
The other king had reigned about three years before him. In his lack of understanding he used to say foolishly: "Why should I send gifts to my slaves?"
And so he sent nothing. Nor was this all: Roman envoys had been sent to his father with gifts and royal letters.
When they reached Antioch, they learned that Khosrow had died and his son had become king.
When our peace-loving Roman emperors learned this, they instructed the envoys to write to the new king and proceed to him.
He arrogantly ordered them to come, but received them with dishonor.
He kept them in distress for a long time, imprisoned and oppressed, until they were close to coming to an end and losing their lives.
Then his magi advised him, and he released them, though he would not even allow them to travel by the direct road.
He sent men with them and ordered them to lead them up through steep and difficult mountains, so that they would perish and die there.
They therefore said to those who were leading them, “If you want to kill us,
why did you not kill us openly at once, instead of bringing us here to die in this misery in these mountains?”
But God helped them, and they escaped. These things were related to the emperor and to everyone, revealing that man's wickedness and lack of understanding.
The first reason the peace was broken was that the Persian Armenians went over to the Romans.
Then a second cause of bitter hostility arose: the Roman emperor sent envoys to those barbarian peoples beyond the Persian territories,
the people called Turks. There were also many other reasons why the Persians fell into distress and hostility.
For Emperor Justin himself had sent envoys to those called Turks in the seventh year of his reign,
including one of the leading men, named Zemarchus. Never before had a Roman embassy been sent to these great and powerful peoples.
So when that envoy held them back in the cities for a whole year, as he related:
And one of the kings of these nations learned—there were, it was said, eight other great kings farther inland than he was—
that an embassy of the Romans had been sent to them. Immediately he was astonished and shaken, and suddenly fell into deep mourning and bitter weeping.
This became still worse when he received the envoys and saw them standing before him for a long time, while no one dared to speak to him.
As others were recounting how bitterly he was weeping, and none of his nobles dared to speak to him, we fell on our faces before him
and told the interpreters to say to him, “We ask you, O king: is it because you have seen us, sent to you by your brother, the emperor of the Romans,
that you are weeping like this?” When he heard this, he wept still more bitterly, again for a long time,
without speaking a single word to us for two hours. Then he quieted his sobbing a little and said to us,
“So that you may know the reason for my mourning and weeping now, I will tell you. We have received this tradition from our ancestors and our families:
‘Whenever you see envoys from the land of the Romans in these regions, know and be certain that the whole world is passing away and being dissolved.
All kingdoms will come to an end, and all people will destroy one another with the sword, immediately, in those very times.’
Now, when I saw you, I remembered these things. That is why I mourned and wept.” After we had spoken at length before him,
they brought out many gifts of gold, silver and pearls, along with splendid royal garments, and presented them to him. When he saw them he was amazed.
He accepted them and immediately set apart those among them that were large and magnificent, saying, “These belong to a great king.” Now there happened to be Persian envoys there.
He asked the Roman envoys: "Is it really true, what the Persians told me, that the king of the Romans is our slave?"
and pays us tribute like a servant’?” When Zemarchus heard this, he answered him,
“They are lying in saying this. Many emperors of the Romans have come down, devastated their country, and taken it captive.
For example, when Trajan, emperor of the Romans, came down, he conquered and subjugated them so thoroughly that to this day
they shake and tremble before the statue he erected for himself in their country. To this day, not one of them dares to pass before it while riding.
Let them be summoned, and we will confront them in person, and they will be unable to deny it.” Then the king gave orders, and they came. He said to them,
“Did you not tell me, ‘The emperor of the Romans is our servant’? Yet, according to what these men say,
to this day you are subject even to the statue of the emperor of the Romans that he erected for himself in your country, and you tremble before it.
How, then, are these men your servants, when you tremble before the statue of the emperor of the Romans and are subject to it? Is this true?”
They said to him, “Yes, my lord, it is true. There is a statue of him in our country.” But he said to them,
“Why did you lie and deceive me?” And he swore, “Were it not that I would become like you, I would have taken off your heads at once.” And so he dismissed them in anger.
When they returned to their king, they told him that they had found Roman envoys there and that these had exposed their falsehood because of the statue of Trajan.
When he could not get us to renounce, he grew angry with us and dismissed us in a rage. When the Persian heard these things, he was shaken and embittered.
He gave orders, and the tyrant’s expression changed because of this, and he became still more fierce in his hostility.
For he thought that the Romans were stirring up these peoples against them, although he himself had bestowed greater honors on them than the Romans had.
This is how these things were handled, as the envoys related. Only small parts of it have been written down.
Those Roman envoys returned after two years,
recounting great and astonishing things about the vast numbers of these peoples, the wonders of those lands, their arrangements, and the orderly nature of their way of life.
Now this long-haired people, called the Avars, came and appeared in Roman territory in the days of Emperor Justinian.
When he received their envoys, he enriched them with gold and silver, clothing, belts, and golden saddles,
and other things that he gave them and sent through them to their leaders, so that they would be astonished and send others again.
He also gave gifts to these others in turn and enriched them, so that they repeatedly sent envoys on various pretexts.
Not only that, but they formed companies and came, and he gave gifts to them all, loaded them up, and they went away.
He believed that through them he would subdue all his enemies, until complaints against him grew loud
from the entire senate and the whole city: “Look, he is emptying the empire and giving it away to the barbarians!”
Thus, when he departed this world and Justin, his sister’s son, became emperor, one company of those who used to come was there, expecting to load up and leave as usual.
After a few days they went in to Justin and said to him, “Give us what the man who died used to give us, and let us leave for our king.”
But Emperor Justin, who had himself been one of those distressed and complaining about how much they were taking and carrying away from the empire, said to them:
“You will no longer load up and carry things away from the empire without giving anything in return. You will take nothing from me and carry it away.”
When they began threatening them, he became furious and said:
“You dead dogs! Are you threatening the Roman Empire? Know that I will shave the hair off all of you
and take your scalps as well!” He gave orders, and they were seized and put in chains.
He had them taken out of the city, and they were taken across and imprisoned in Chalcedon. There were about three hundred men.
An army was stationed there along with scribones and scholarii to guard them for six months.
Finally, he released them and sent them away, threatening them with these words: “If I see any of you here, or anywhere in my realm, you will no longer be allowed to live.”
They were so frightened of him that they kept quiet and did not appear before him again. Eventually, however, they sent him envoys offering friendship and submission,
and promising to do whatever he commanded them. In this way they remained friends throughout his lifetime.
And because they were a powerful people, they became still richer and stronger through the many northern peoples whom they conquered and devastated.
Finally, beyond the great river called the Danube, they fell upon another powerful people, the Gepids,
They destroyed them and took over their land. Then they settled and spread out in that good land.
Later, pretending to be friends, they deceitfully sent envoys to Emperor Justin, asking him—that is, their king was asking him—
to send him engineers and builders to build him a residence, a palace, and a bathhouse. And he did indeed send them.
When they had gone and built him a palace and a bathhouse and finished them, they asked to be released and return home. Then he revealed his deceit and showed the treachery in his heart.
He seized them and drew his sword against them, saying, “Unless you use your skill to build a bridge across the Danube,
so that we can cross wherever we wish, not one of you will live. I will cut off your heads immediately.”
Under this pressure, they said to him, “Who can, or has ever been able to, build a bridge over a river that is like a sea?
Besides, even if they had been able to do this, it was against the Roman state.
and the emperor himself would kill us. Whether we die or live, we cannot do this.”
Immediately he cut off the heads of two of them. Then the rest, terrified of death,
promised, “If you bring us many large, strong timbers, we will do it, so that we do not die.”
Then a great many people went out and cut down many strong, large trees.
Thus, compelled by the threat of death by the sword, they devised a plan and built a very strong bridge. When Emperor Justin had reigned for thirteen years, he departed this world.
The victorious Tiberius, who had served alongside him as Caesar for four years, then appeared as sole emperor after him.
This [event], which wore down the whole state not a little, and the deed that took place, happened in the third year of his reign, after the death of Justin.
He tried every possible means to cut the bridge, but so far he had been unable to do so. They still hold it and remain there,
demanding that he either give them the city of Sirmium, on this side of the river, to live in, or else they would wage war against him and devastate his state.
But he was not at all inclined to give it to them. And now they are gathered together and waiting, ready to rise up for war if they find an opportunity.
They also built another bridge, as is reported—something that had never happened before. This too they did as they prepared for evil.
In the third year after the death of Emperor Justin and of the reign of the victorious Tiberius, the accursed people of the Slavs came out,
And they overran the whole of Hellas and the regions of Thessalonica and of all Thrace, and they captured many cities and forts.
They devastated and burned, took captives, and gained control of the land. They settled there freely, as though it were their own, without fear, for four years now.
And still, because the emperor was occupied with the Persian war and had sent all his armies to the east, they overran the land and settled in it.
And they spread through it for a time, as long as God allowed them. They ravaged, burned, and took captives.
They even reached the outer wall and carried off all the emperor’s horse herds, many thousands, along with the other animals.
And even to this day, which is the year eight hundred and ninety-five, they remain encamped and settled there.
In these Roman territories they live without anxiety or fear. They take captives, kill, and burn.
They have grown rich and acquired gold and silver, herds of horses, and many weapons.
They have learned to fight better than the Romans—savage men who had not dared to show themselves outside the woods and the dense cover of the trees,
and who had not known what a weapon was, apart from two or three small spears, that is, throwing spears.
After the great devastation that had taken place in both the Roman and Persian states, both sides wanted to negotiate peace between the two kingdoms.
So that it was being negotiated through the bishops of Nisibis and of Resh'aina and the others, and through Zachariah the sophist from the frontier wall of the Romans.
Finally, a certain one-eyed Persian frontier commander became an obstacle. Trusting in his strength, puffed up and boasting of his prowess, he said to his king,
“Do not give in to the Romans or make peace with them. I will cross over immediately and devastate them all, and I will conquer all their territories.
I will spend the winter in Antioch.” Trusting in his boasting, the king neglected the peace negotiations, becoming puffed up himself.
So this frontier commander, whose name was Tamkhosrau, gathered his forces and advanced against Tella-Mauzalat, where there were high-ranking generals.
And the commanders of the armies that were in it. And they arrived and surrounded the city; then the stratelates went out to meet him.
and especially a brave and mighty man whose name was Constantine.
The day before, he had captured one of their spies and questioned him about the frontier commander Tamkhosrau: what he looked like,
And in whatever place the army was going and was found, he, when he learned of it, went out to battle on one side and saw the marzban in the middle of the army,
He hurled himself forward in a charge and plunged into the Persian army, heading straight for Tamkhosrau.
and he struck him with a lance, uprooted him and threw him from his horse. And he turned with the lance, struck him and pierced him.
The other Persians surrounded him and killed Constantine there as well, a faithful Christian and a fighting man.
When the Persians saw that the man on whom they relied more than on the king had been killed,
the man who had boasted that he would immediately take the city in a single assault and make his quarters there, and when all the Roman forces surrounded them on every side,
they turned and fled. The Romans and Arabs pursued them, slaughtering and striking down many of them—many thousands, according to what is reported.
Because we are not certain about this, and in order to refrain from [?] falsehood, we have not recorded it as it was reported.
Nevertheless, it became known that many of them had fallen. It was also reported that three other leaders of theirs had been killed.
And all their arrogance was put to shame. They fled and went and encamped by the river called Beth Washi.
They stayed there for three months, watching and preparing for battle. And when they were unable to stand against the Romans,
they returned to their own country in shame, since the things they had planned had not happened as they intended. These events unfolded in this way.
Concerning Maurice, then, even though mention of the matter was made above: this man, when Justinian the patrician, son of Germanus,
who had been placed over all the commanders and armies in the East, departed this world, and the commanders of the armies would not submit to one another—
But the merciful King Tiberius, because he had been his notary with him, for this reason, when he became king, promoted him,
and gave him the position of count of the excubitors. Then he sent him as head over all the stratelates and the great commanders of the Roman armies,
throughout the whole East. He gave him authority over all the arrangements for war, to wage war, to make peace, and to do whatever he wished.
so that, when he had received this command, he went out with a large army, with excubitors and scribones, and reached the land of Cappadocia.
from which he himself came, from the city of Arabissus, he first selected many young men from that country and enlisted them as Roman soldiers.
He did likewise in the district of Hanzit in Armenia, and in Syria when he reached there.
First he went and attacked the city of Citharizon. The whole country of the Persians was shaken at the first report of him.
Now the frontier governor who was keeping watch in Persian Armenia, when he was shaken by the report of him and wanted to escape from him by a pretext,
deceitfully sent word to the commanders stationed in Theodosiopolis: “How long shall we sit waiting for one another?
In thirty days, let us prepare for battle and fight, and find out who wins and who is defeated.”
When these words were spoken, the commanders sent word to Count Maurice. He ordered them to send back to him: “Look, we are ready.”
While the Romans relied on this reply, the frontier governor and his army fled that very night and left there, passing through their own country.
They came and crossed into Roman territory opposite Martyropolis, and began devastating, burning, taking captives, and killing,
Throughout the whole region of Sophene and the region of the Amidenes. And they came as far as Amida, surrounded it and besieged it for three days.
When they saw that they could not overcome the strength of the city, they demanded that gold be given to them as the city's ransom,
so that they would not burn its surroundings. But the inhabitants did not believe them, reasoning that whether they received anything or not, they would certainly burn them.
So they became angry and burned all the churches and all the monasteries, large and small, and everything else outside the city.
They ranged as far as they could. Thus, within fifteen days they plundered, took captives, and crossed back into their own country, in haste and in great fear of the Romans.
When Count Maurice finally learned of this, he was embittered, took his army, and set out for Syria,
pursuing them, but he did not catch them. Then the Roman armies, in fury and anger, fell upon the districts of Arzanene.
They ravaged, burned, and devastated all the regions, took their people captive, and brought them into Roman territory.
As we related in the preceding account. All the captives who were brought across from there were sent, by the emperor’s command, to the island of Cyprus.
They were distributed among the cities and villages, and they remain there to this day.
While, then, the bulk of the Roman army was facing Persian Armenia, with two stratelates,
John and Cours. The Persian army, too, was stationed opposite them. But, as we have also related above,
the Roman army split apart, and about fifty thousand of them stood aside, angry and grumbling, saying,
“Unless we receive our allowances in full and the numbers assigned to each of us are made known to us,
so that we can be sure of our positions, not one of us will go out to battle, and we will not fight anyone.”
so that when these things became known to King Tiberius, at once and without delay he sent there the curator of the royal house of Hormisdas, whose name was Domentziolus,
giving him a great deal of gold to distribute to them, to satisfy them and calm them. And so they were made ready for battle.
At that same time, the Persian marzbans sent word to the Roman commanders: “Why are we sitting opposite one another, watching one another like women?
Let us go out onto the plain and fight one another.” When Cours, the commander of the Romans, heard this, being a wise man who had served the great Narses,
and had gained experience with him in great battles in Roman territory, he sent them this reply: “We cannot fight now,
because our whole army is not here at present. But if you come against us, we will meet you with whatever strength our God gives us.”
When the people of the Magi received this message, they advanced with great confidence, no longer being wary of the Romans or afraid of them.
That very day, Cours quietly prepared his own force of only about twenty thousand and went out by night, at the first light of dawn,
While these, without forethought, were beginning, rushing about and lying down [?], he fell upon them like a fire let loose in a thicket and like a flame that burns up mountains.
He stunned them and threw them into confusion, and slaughtered them, except for a few who escaped. He captured and bound many.
He also captured one of the marzbans and his son. Thus he plundered their entire camp and returned in great triumph, taking their weapons and horses.
Now after the death of Khosrow, king of the Persians, his son Hormizd, who became king after him,
followed the vile custom of those who become kings there, of killing all their brothers: he too killed some of his brothers,
and blinded others. But there was one whom, they say, his father had wanted to become king, but whom their entire senate rejected and refused to accept.
As the story is told, Khosrow himself gave this man provisions and sent him away while he was still alive, saying to him, “Go, my son, flee while I am alive, so that you do not die.”
After he fled, many things were said about him. His countrymen believed and heard reports that he was in many different places.
So a certain impostor, a crafty young man from among the Persians, went and fabricated stories and produced evidence to make people believe that he was the son of Khosrow who had fled.
And so he came to the commanders of the Roman armies in Persian Armenia and told them that he wished to submit to the Roman Empire.
“If the Roman emperor receives me and gives me an army,” he said, “I will conquer all the armies and territories of the Persians.
And I will bring my brother Hormizd, who seized my kingdom, in chains and hand him over to the Roman emperor.”
When the commanders of the Roman armies had questioned him extensively, and he had also produced many people who testified about him,
that he was the king’s son who had fled from his brother, they believed him and wrote to Emperor Tiberius about him and about all the inquiries they had made concerning him.
They also wrote that they had found people who knew him and testified that he was the king’s son, and that he was destitute.
When the victorious emperor received this report and accepted everything the army commanders had written to him,
he immediately sent envoys with much gold and silver, many splendid garments, and many horses and mules, to honor him and transport him.
He ordered that he should reach the imperial city escorted with ceremony through all the territories and cities by all the provincial governors. And this was done.
He traveled through the territories like a king, with great ceremony and lavish honors. The emperor also sent high-ranking dignitaries to welcome him.
When he reached Chalcedon, across the water from the imperial city, he was ordered to remain there, since the emperor intended to investigate him thoroughly.
For there was an aspatar [?] of the king of the Persians who had come and been handed over to him; and he knew this man, together with those to whom the envoys had gone down.
The emperor ordered them to cross over to him and see whether they too knew him, and to question him in case he was an impostor. “We must not be made fools of,” he said.
When they crossed over and saw him, they did not recognize him. But that Persian sword-bearer questioned him extensively,
and could find no way to establish the truth of his claims. Meanwhile, the man was sitting on an elevated seat like a king.
Then the sword-bearer seized him by the hair, pulled him up, and threw him down, saying,
“You [?], deserving of death! You sit on an elevated throne while the empire’s dignitaries stand before you!”
He also struck him on the neck. In this way he exposed his imposture, and the man could not extricate himself or establish the truth of his claims.
The emperor then gave orders, and he was lodged in a place, without being treated as his imposture deserved.
Instead, he even ordered that expenses be provided for him and those with him. The emperor himself never saw him.
It was said that more than three centenaria had been spent on him. In the end, he also became a Christian.
Now, while the barbarian people of the Avars were gathered and holding the two bridges they had built,
and remained there threatening war and devastation against Roman territories, they sent word to Emperor Tiberius: “If you wish to make us your friends,
give us Sirmium so that we may settle in it with your consent. Otherwise, we will take it without your consent, and we will be your enemies.”
But the emperor kept putting them off with words and various promises, since he was entirely unwilling to give it to them.
But he was secretly sending envoys to the Lombards, to hire them and bring them against the others from behind, and to other peoples as well.
While these people were putting pressure on him, he decided not to reveal his intention to them. He sent Narses, the chief imperial sword-bearer, to speak with them and stall them.
He took a great deal of gold, both his own and the empire’s. He was secretly instructed not to hurry on his journey.
If these peoples came, he was to receive them and attack them, and, if possible, destroy them.
Meanwhile, he sent them this message: “We have now sent the illustrious Narses, our sword-bearer, to come and speak with you and make peace with you.”
So the illustrious Narses, the sword-bearer, left the imperial capital with great pomp, accompanied by a large force, an enormous amount of gold, and garments of various kinds.
After loading many ships with goods of every kind, he began the voyage across the fearsome Sea of Pontus. One ship carried most of the gold and many other things.
Also aboard it were one of his officers and other trusted men, who were stationed there to guard its contents. It sank on the very first day of their voyage.
When he learned this, after leaving the sea near the River Danube, his distress brought on a severe illness.
After a bitter decline lasting some time, his end overtook him, and he died in great suffering. All his plans came to nothing.
He had accomplished absolutely nothing. Many other things happened afterward in connection with the inquiry into his actions.

Since the things intended to be accomplished through Narses had not been done, and to prevent these peoples from pressing harder, the emperor was forced to send another man, named Callistratus, the prefect
of the praetorium, to the Avars. He went and handed that city over to them.
For he had decided that this was more advantageous than its being taken by war and force, after it had endured two years of distress and bitter famine.
Their bitter distress was such that they ate even cats, after eating all the livestock, all the other animals, and everything else.
It was no less severe than what Scripture tells us once happened in Samaria.
People also spoke of the compassion these barbarians showed toward those suffering the torments of famine there.
These acts deserve admiration and bring condemnation upon Christians, who show no kindness to their fellows and have no compassion for their own flesh and blood.
They said that when these men entered and saw the deadly suffering of the people in the city, they had compassion on them and gave them bread to eat and wine to drink.
But because of the ravages of famine throughout those two whole years, the people would snatch the food and eat it, and then quickly die without warning.
Thus those who survived went into exile and left the city, while the barbarians took possession of it and settled there.
As has been said, after the barbarians had captured the city of the Christians and stayed in it for the space of one year,
a fire broke out in the city of Sirmium—God knows through what agency—and suddenly swept through it and burned the whole city.
Because the barbarians did not know how to stop or extinguish it, they all fled naked and left the city.
The whole city burned and was destroyed. There were many things in its story that deserved to be recorded.
Because the many accounts would be so lengthy, we have left most of them aside.
So, briefly and in sequence, we have related some of what happened in the earlier wars, as we were able to learn through careful investigation:
We recorded the campaign of the illustrious patrician Marcian against Nisibis and the events that happened there.
Then we described Khosrow’s crossing into Roman territory with his armies, his capture of Dara, and also that of the city of Apamea, and the rest.
After these things, we described the arrival of the victorious Maurice in the East with great pomp, and the fear of him that fell upon the people of the Magi.
and because, thinking that they could deceive him through foolishness, they crossed into Roman territory from the side toward Maipherqat,
and they burned and passed through in great haste in fifteen days, in the land of the Sophenians.
They came against Amida, and when they saw that they could not capture the city, in their frenzy they barbarously set fires and burned all its surroundings:
churches, monasteries, and the rest. They took captives and hurried back to their own country.
We also related how, when Count Maurice learned of these things, he was stirred to fierce anger and pursued them, but did not overtake them.
He rushed straight to the territory of Arzanene, burned, uprooted, and took captives, and carried off all the people of Arzanene whom he had not killed.
He brought them over into Roman territory. They were all sent to the island of Cyprus. Meanwhile, he captured fortresses there.
He seized one called Phum and stationed a Roman force in it. There was also another Persian fortress opposite it, called Klimar; he accepted its ransom and left it alone.
They remained opposite one another, made peace with one another, and traded with one another without fear of each other.
Count Maurice himself likewise undertook to build a fortress on a high and rugged mountain called Shamkart.
The fortress itself was therefore also named Shamkart. He stationed Romans in it, assigned them provisions, and attended to everything it needed.
This Shamkart is in Roman territory. He left its construction in the hands of an engineer who had defected to him from Persian territory.
Now, beyond the River Kallath, which lies along the frontier opposite Martyropolis, there was an inaccessible mountain.
For a long time, that uprooted people of the Magi had been planning to build a fortress on it.
But there was a treaty between the Romans and the Persians that neither side should be permitted to build within a certain number of miles of the frontier.
The Romans therefore opposed them and would not allow them to build. Indeed, many times it was built and then torn down.
At one point, however, as we have already explained, the Persians found an opportunity, built the fortress, and occupied it.
Years later, the Roman armies attacked it and surrounded it.
This was the stratelates whose name was Ola [?]. And for a long time he had been surrounded and they had been besieging him.
until those living in it were afflicted by hunger and thirst, so that they were close to losing their lives in this world.
Then, when they saw their distress, they asked to be given an assurance that they would not be killed or captured and taken prisoner, and that they could pass into Roman territory.
They would hand the fortress over to them and leave it. The commanders agreed to this and gave them their word. They opened it, and all of them came down from it.
And when they came out, found water and drank, they were falling down and dying at once, so that only a few of them got out and went away.
The general and his army went up and demolished the entire fortress. They left no stone upon another, but tore it down and threw it down from the mountain.
The other commanders and the bulk of the army also gathered there. They remained stationed separately in various places, keeping watch against one another.
At the time when Aqba was captured, which was in the year eight hundred and ninety-four, a Persian envoy was sent to our emperor, the emperor of the Romans.
They began to discuss peace, and the envoy was warmly received. It was agreed that a Roman envoy should be sent to the king of the Persians.
